pages.html:
# Reading Journal: Student Guidelines

Grade band: 6 to 8. Voice: direct, short sentences, second person.

This is the student-facing guidelines text. Place it on the module's first page or pin it as a Canvas page. The builder fills the few bracketed course-specific fields.

---

## What the Reading Journal is

Your Reading Journal is one Word document that you keep for the whole module. It is your organizer. Your vocabulary, your reading notes and answers, your notes on how the author writes, and your growing project idea all live in this one file. You build it a little every week.

You do not turn it in every week. Your teacher looks at it closely twice: once around the middle of the module and once at the end. That review is called the Reading Journal Check.

## How to make your copy

1. Open the Reading Journal document for this module from the assignment in Canvas. Word will open your own copy in your school M365 account. 2. If your teacher did not hand you a copy through Canvas, open Word from office.com using your school account (not a personal account), open the module's Reading Journal template, and use File > Save As to make your own copy. 3. Name your file like this: LastName_[COURSECODE]_ReadingJournal_[MODULESHORTNAME]. Example: Garcia_GT_ReadingJournal_Module1.

## Where to save it

Save it in your OneDrive course folder so it is easy to find all module long:

Optima > ELA > [Course_Semester]

Keep the journal in the same folder as your Quick Writes. Do not save it to your desktop or a personal account, and do not start a new copy each week. One document, all module.

## How to add to it each week

  • When a lesson says "Add this to the Week ___ section of your Reading Journal," open your journal and go to that week's block in Section 3.
  • Type your answers under the prompts. Do not erase the prompts; answer beneath them.
  • Add the week's vocabulary to the Section 2 table.
  • Add one new dated line to your Section 1 answer to the Module Question.
  • Drop any craft or character notes into Section 4, and add to your project claim in Section 5 when a Quick Write points you there.
  • OneDrive saves your work automatically and keeps a version history, so you will not lose it.

## What the Reading Journal Check looks at

When your teacher reviews your journal, they read three sections:

  • Section 2 (Word Study): Did you add the words, with meanings in your own words and the lines they came from?
  • Section 3 (Weekly Reading Notes and Responses): Did you answer each week's prompts in full sentences, using details from the reading?
  • Section 5 (Toward the Project): Is your claim taking shape, with evidence attached?

You are graded on completeness and honest effort, not on having a perfect answer. The point is steady building. If a week is thin, the check is your signal to catch it up before the project.

Quick reminder: one document, kept in your OneDrive course folder, added to every week. That is the whole habit.

RESEARCH AND JSTOR ACCESS
Finding real sources, and knowing they are real
JStor is a large library of articles that scholars have checked before publishing. This page shows you how to get in. Keep it bookmarked; you will come back to it whenever a lesson asks you to find a source.
🔑 HOW TO LOG IN (OPTIMA SHARED ACCESS)

Go to www.jstor.org and sign in with the Optima account below. This account is for Optima students' coursework only. Please do not share it with anyone outside the school.

Username: optimaonline
Password: wisdom359

There is no separate "off campus" step. This is the same login whether you are at home or anywhere else, because Optima is an online school.

📚 TWO PLACES, ONE LIBRARY
STEP 1 · JSTOR DAILY
daily.jstor.org. No login needed. Short, readable articles written for anyone, and every one links to the real research behind it.
STEP 2 · JSTOR
jstor.org, signed in with the login above. This is the full library: the scholarly article itself, and thousands more like it.
🔍 SEARCH WELL
Use two or three key words, not a full question. "Klondike sled dogs" finds more than "how did dogs help people during the gold rush."
Read the short summary at the top of an article (the abstract) before opening the whole thing. It tells you fast whether the source fits.
⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · AI AND SOURCES
An AI tool can help you turn a question into search words. It cannot tell you what articles actually exist, and it sometimes invents titles and authors that sound real but are not. Only ever use a source you found and opened on JStor yourself.

# Gulliver's Travels: Reading Journal / Module Organizer (M365 Word doc spec)

Module 1 instance, built from the course-shared TEMPLATE. This is the exact spec for the Word document each student copies at the start of Module 1 and keeps in the OneDrive course folder. Hand it out through the Canvas + OneDrive LTI assignment so each student gets their own copy. The five fixed sections match every module of the course.

Hard rules. No em dashes in student-facing text. Name craft terms plainly. Dates carry A.D. or B.C. where relevant.

---

## Document setup and layout

  • File type: Microsoft Word (.docx), from the student's school M365 account.
  • File name: LastName_GT_ReadingJournal_Module1 (example: Garcia_GT_ReadingJournal_Module1).
  • Save location: Optima > ELA > [Course_Semester] in OneDrive.
  • Font: Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12.
  • Headings: Word Heading 1 for each Section; Heading 2 for each week block in Section 3.
  • Page numbers: bottom of the page.
  • Tables: real Word tables for Section 2 and the Section 3 blocks.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading Styles and Inserting a Table (Word).

---

## COVER (first page)

  • Course: 7th Grade English Language Arts
  • Module: Module 1, Gulliver's Travels (Jonathan Swift, 1726)
  • Student name: [student types]
  • Module Question / Theme: How does changing your perspective change what you see, in others and in yourself?

Center the block; course name largest; module question in italics beneath.

---

## SECTION 1: Module Question (your evolving answer)

Heading 1: Section 1, Module Question

The big question for this module is below. You will answer it many times. Do not erase old answers. Add a new dated line each week so you can watch your thinking change.

Module Question: How does changing your perspective change what you see, in others and in yourself?

  • Week 1 answer (date): _______
  • Week 2 answer (date): _______
  • Week 3 answer (date): _______
  • Week 4 answer (date): _______
  • Week 5 answer (date): _______
  • Week 6 answer (date): _______
  • Week 7 answer (date): _______
  • Final answer before the project (date): _______

---

## SECTION 2: Word Study

Heading 1: Section 2, Word Study

Each week you study a small set of words from the reading. Add every word to the table below. Write what it means in your own words, and copy the exact line from the book where you met it.

Insert one Word table with these exact headers, pre-loaded with a divider row per week and empty rows for each word:

| Word | What it means (in your own words) | The line it came from (with chapter) | |------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|

Pre-load these week labels and words (meanings are starter glosses; students rewrite in their own words):

  • Week 1, Part I, Ch. 1 to 2: diminutive, prodigious, conjecture, ingenious, intrepidity
  • Week 2, Part I, Ch. 3 to 6: dexterity, magnificence, animosity, circumspection, vindicate
  • Week 3, Part I, Ch. 7 to 8: impeachment, treason, lenity, resentment, ignominious
  • Week 4, Part II, Ch. 1 to 5: prodigious, diminutive, mortification, supplicating, ingenious
  • Week 5, Part II, Ch. 6 to 8: levee, panegyric, pernicious, abominate, prodigious
  • Week 6, Part IV, Ch. 1 to 8: conjecture, antipathy, abominable, avarice, benevolence
  • Week 7, Part IV, Ch. 9 to 12: expedient, tranquillity, antipathy, veracity, magnanimous

---

## SECTION 3: Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

Heading 1: Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

This is the heart of your journal. There is one block per week. When a lesson says "Add this to the Week ___ section of your Reading Journal," this is where it goes. Each week block has two parts: the reading-response prompts (answer these in full sentences) and a space for your own notes.

Create one Heading 2 block per week, exactly as below.

### Heading 2: Week 1, Part I, Ch. 1 to 2

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. Describe how Gulliver ends up in Lilliput. What happens to him between the shipwreck and waking up on the ground? 2. The Lilliputians are tiny, but they manage to control Gulliver. Give two specific things they do, and explain what those details show about them. 3. Satire uses humor or exaggeration to make a point. Choose one moment from Chapter 1 that you think is satire, and explain what Swift might be poking fun at.

My reading notes (characters, surprising lines, questions): _______

### Heading 2: Week 2, Part I, Ch. 3 to 6

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. In Chapter 3, how do candidates win a high government office? Name the detail, then explain what it suggests about how Lilliput chooses its leaders. 2. In Chapter 4, what started the war between Lilliput and Blefuscu? Describe the cause, then explain what Swift might want readers to think about real wars. 3. The emperor describes himself with grand titles, such as "delight and terror of the universe." He rules a kingdom about twelve miles across. What is the gap between his words and the truth, and what does that gap show?

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 3, Part I, Ch. 7 to 8

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. List two of the charges in the articles of impeachment against Gulliver. Stick to what the text reports, not how Gulliver feels about it. 2. The court calls blinding Gulliver an act of mercy. Find one word or phrase Gulliver uses that shows how he wants you to judge that mercy. What is his opinion doing to your view of the court? 3. We only hear this trial from Gulliver. Pick one moment and explain how a Lilliputian official might describe that same moment differently. What does the gap tell you about trusting a single narrator?

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 4, Part II, Ch. 1 to 5

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. Describe how Gulliver ends up among the giants. What does the farmer do when he first finds him, and how is that different from how the Lilliputians treated Gulliver? 2. Find one ordinary thing that becomes dangerous or strange because Gulliver is now tiny (for example, the grain field, the cat, the dinner table, or the rats). Describe it and explain how the change in size makes it feel different. 3. Gulliver says that "nothing is great or little otherwise than by comparison." In your own words, what does he mean, and how does Part II show it to be true?

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 5, Part II, Ch. 6 to 8

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. Pick one of the king's questions about England (for example, about bought seats, bribed judges, or the standing army). What flaw in England does that question quietly expose? 2. The king calls Gulliver's countrymen "the most pernicious race of little odious vermin." Explain why the king reaches this verdict, using what Gulliver actually told him. 3. Theme is a big idea an author builds across a story. In one or two sentences, state the theme of this chapter in your own words, then name one detail that supports it.

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 6, Part IV, Ch. 1 to 8

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. Describe one clear way the Houyhnhnms and the Yahoos are opposites. Give one detail about each side. 2. Gulliver tries hard to hide that he is shaped like a Yahoo. Why is this so upsetting to him? Use a detail from the reading. 3. The Houyhnhnms have no word for lying. What does that one missing word tell you about how they live? Explain in your own words.

My reading notes: _______

### Heading 2: Week 7, Part IV, Ch. 9 to 12

Reading-response prompts (answer in full sentences): 1. Foreshadowing is a clue that hints at something later. Find the sentence in Chapter 9 where Gulliver hints that trouble is coming. Copy a few words of it, and explain what it warns you about. 2. The clue is dropped in the middle of a calm tour of Houyhnhnm life. Why do you think Swift placed it there instead of saving it for a dramatic moment? 3. Now that you have seen the clue, how do you expect Gulliver's happy life with the horses to end? Make one prediction and tie it to the clue.

My reading notes: _______

---

## SECTION 4: Craft, Characters, Theme (running notes)

Heading 1: Section 4, Craft, Characters, Theme

Use this section all module long. When a lesson names a craft move (point of view, foreshadowing, figurative language) or you notice how Gulliver changes, add a short note here with the chapter. You will pull from this section when you build your project.

  • Craft moves I noticed: (term, what it was, the chapter)
  • Characters and how they change: (especially Gulliver, who is different by the end of Part IV)
  • Theme ideas: (a big idea Swift seems to be building, and one detail that supports it)

---

## SECTION 5: Toward the Project (your developing claim)

Heading 1: Section 5, Toward the Project

Your module project asks you to make a claim and back it up. Build that claim here, a little at a time, using your Quick Writes (especially Quick Writes 5, 6, and 7). By the end you should have a claim plus two or three pieces of evidence.

  • The project question: Which voyage best reveals Swift's view of humanity, and what does the book say about the folly of human pride?
  • My claim (a sentence that answers the question): _______
  • Evidence 1 (a detail or quotation, cited in MLA format: Swift plus part and chapter): _______ . Why it supports my claim: _______
  • Evidence 2: _______ . Why it supports my claim: _______
  • Evidence 3 (optional): _______ . Why it supports my claim: _______
  • A reason someone might disagree, and my response: _______
  • Works Cited entry (add once, at the end): _Swift, Jonathan. Gulliver's Travels. 1726._

---

## Reminder line for the bottom of the document

Keep this document in your OneDrive course folder all module long. Your teacher reviews Sections 2, 3, and 5 at the Reading Journal Check (around Week 4 and at the end of the module). You are not turning it in every week; you are building it every week.

Week 1
Word Study: Words from Lilliput
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
diminutive (very small): “...the intrepidity of these diminutive mortals...”
prodigious (huge, amazing): “...so prodigious a creature as I must appear to them.”
conjecture (a guess from evidence): “...which I conjectured was about eight o’clock...”
ingenious (clever and inventive): “...being a most ingenious people...”
intrepidity (fearless courage): “...I could not sufficiently wonder at the intrepidity...”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
conjecture comes from the Latin root ject, meaning “throw,” joined with con-, meaning “together.” To conjecture is to throw ideas together from the evidence you have, which is why it means an educated guess.
ingenious comes from the Latin root gen, meaning “born” or “produced” (the same root in genius and generate). An ingenious person seems to produce clever ideas naturally.
intrepidity joins the Latin prefix in-, meaning “not,” with the root trepid, meaning “trembling with fear” (the same root in trepidation). Intrepidity is literally the state of not trembling: fearless courage.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what prodigious means in the line “...so prodigious a creature as I must appear to them”? Think it through before you check the definition.

2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “...so prodigious a creature as I must appear to them.”
Your rewrite: “...such an enormous, towering creature as I must have seemed to them.”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly.

☐

☐

In Chapter 1, Gulliver is enormous and the Lilliputians are tiny, yet they control him. In VR you can stand inside that size difference and feel it. Annotate a Satire Object: The Pride of Lilliput
Solo VR activity · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
Chapters 1 and 2 are full of small things treated grandly: a golden helmet, a three-inch royal sword, a solemn council, an imperial commission. You will build one of those objects in VR, then label it with real text details that show the gap between how small it is and how proud Lilliput is of it. Save your work: it becomes raw material for your Module 1 project on scale and human pride.

Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · Chapters 1 and 2 (reread the emperor and council passages if you want the details fresh).
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and open the class virtual space for this course. Choose any setting you like, such as a study room, a gallery, or an open field. You only need a flat surface and room to place one object and two labels.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Choose one piece of Lilliputian pride or ceremony from Chapter 1 or 2: the emperor’s golden helmet with its plume, his three-inch royal sword, the imperial commission for daily food, or the ceremony of the court in its embroidered clothes.

📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
dexterity (skill with the hands or body): “...wherein they exceed all nations I have known, both for dexterity and magnificence.” (Ch. 3)
magnificence (grand, impressive splendor): “...both for dexterity and magnificence.” (Ch. 3)
animosity (strong hostility or hatred): “The animosities between these two parties run so high...” (Ch. 4)
circumspection (careful caution before acting): “I walked with the utmost circumspection, to avoid treading on any stragglers...” (Ch. 4)
vindicate (to clear someone of blame; to defend a reputation): “I am here obliged to vindicate the reputation of an excellent lady...” (Ch. 6)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
circumspection comes from the Latin roots circum, meaning “around,” and spect, meaning “look” (the same root in inspect and spectator). To act with circumspection is to look around carefully before acting.
magnificence comes from the Latin roots magn, meaning “great” (as in magnify), and fic, meaning “make.” Magnificence is the quality of something made on a great, impressive scale.
animosity comes from the Latin root anim, meaning “spirit” or “strong feeling” (the same root in animate and animal). Animosity is a strong, hostile feeling toward someone.

Word Study: Words from the Trial and the Escape
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
impeachment (the act of formally accusing a public official of serious misconduct): “Articles of impeachment against Quinbus Flestrin.” (Ch. 7)
treason (the crime of betraying your own country or its ruler): “...he was charged with high treason...” (Ch. 7)
lenity (gentleness or mercy in punishing): “...this was looked upon as the greatest lenity...” (Ch. 7)
resentment (bitter anger at being treated unfairly): “...the resentment of his majesty...” (Ch. 7)
ignominious (bringing public shame or disgrace): “...rather than suffer so ignominious a death...” (Ch. 7)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
treason comes from the Latin roots trans, meaning “across,” and dare, meaning “to give.” Treason is literally handing your loyalty across to the other side: betrayal of your own country or ruler.
lenity comes from the Latin root len, meaning “soft” or “mild” (the same root in lenient). Lenity is a soft, mild way of punishing someone.
ignominious joins the Latin prefix in- (spelled ig- here), meaning “not,” with the root nomin, meaning “name” (the same root in nominate). Something ignominious costs a person their good name.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what impeachment means in the line “Articles of impeachment against Quinbus Flestrin”? Think it through before you check the definition.

1
Add all five words and their meanings to the vocabulary section of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “...the resentment of his majesty...”
Your rewrite: “...the bitter anger the emperor felt...”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the book.

The Other Side of the Story: A Point-of-View Recording
Solo VR activity · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Chapter 7, we hear about Gulliver’s treason trial only from Gulliver. In VR you will stage that scene, then step into a Lilliputian’s shoes and record the same moment from their point of view. This is point-of-view practice you will reuse in your Module 1 project, where you contrast how the same person looks tiny in one land and giant in another.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · your copy of Chapter 7 (reread the trial pages if you want the charges fresh).
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual setting for this course. Choose any setting you like that gives you an indoor space with room to place a few objects, such as a hall or a chamber where a court might meet. You only need room to set up a small scene.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Build the trial scene. Place one large object to stand for Gulliver, the Man-Mountain, and a cluster of small objects to stand for the Lilliputian court and his accusers, Bolgolam and Flimnap.
2
Add two labels or sticky notes. On the first, write the charge against Gulliver in his own words, as he tells it. On the second, write how a frightened Lilliputian official would describe the same giant and the same threat.
3
Stand among the small objects, at the court’s height, and look up at the giant. Notice how the scene feels from down there. From a Lilliputian’s view, a creature who could crush the palace might look less like a wronged hero and more like a danger.
4
Record the trial as the Lilliputian. Speaking as a court official, tell the story of the charges against the Man-Mountain in three or four sentences, in your new point of view.

Record a short video inside VR of your scene and your spoken Lilliputian account, or take a screenshot of your staged scene with both labels visible. Upload it to Canvas. If your setup does not allow capture, you may type a short written reflection instead. Either way, add two or three sentences: how does the trial change when you tell it from the Lilliputian’s side?

☐
The scene shows a giant Gulliver and the small Lilliputian court.
☐
Two labels give two points of view: Gulliver’s and a Lilliputian official’s.
☐
A video, screenshot, or written reflection is uploaded, plus the short response.

This is a solo activity, and the only VR activity this short week. The goal is the shift in point of view, not a polished set, so steer students away from chasing perfect props. A finished submission shows the giant-versus-court scale, two labels for the two viewpoints, and a spoken or written retelling from the Lilliputian side. Save these recordings: they are direct raw material for the Module 1 project on scale and human pride.

Word Study: Words from Brobdingnag
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
prodigious (huge, enormous): “...he waded not much deeper than his knees, and took prodigious strides.”
diminutive (very small): “...the people were as diminutive with respect to them, as they were to me.”
mortification (a feeling of shame or humbled pride): “...what a mortification it must prove to me, to appear as inconsiderable in this nation.”
supplicating (begging, pleading): “...place my hands together in a supplicating posture...”
ingenious (clever and inventive): “This man was a most ingenious artist...”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
diminutive comes from the Latin root min, meaning “small” or “less” (the same root in minus and diminish). Diminutive describes something reduced to a very small size.
mortification comes from the Latin root mort, meaning “death” (the same root in mortal and immortal), joined with fic, meaning “make.” It originally meant to figuratively kill off pride or feeling, which is why it now means a deep, humbled shame.
supplicating comes from the Latin roots sub-, meaning “under,” and plic, meaning “fold” (the same root in complicate). To supplicate is literally to fold yourself under someone, bending low to beg.

🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Week 1 you staged Gulliver as a giant lying among tiny Lilliputians. Now the scale flips. In Brobdingnag, Gulliver is the small one, dwarfed by a dinner table, a cat, and a curious child. In VR you will build that same moment from the other side and feel what it is like to be tiny. This is the mirror image of your Week 1 scene, and together the two scenes are the heart of your Module 1 project on scale and human pride. Save your work.

Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · your memory of Part II, Chapters 1 to 3 (reread the dinner-table scene or the cat scene if you want details fresh).

Two labels each name a real detail from Part II, Chapters 1 to 3.

assignments.html:
# Reading Journal Check: Gulliver's Travels (Tier 2 checkpoints)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). Two occurrences per module: a mid-module check around Week 4 and an end-of-module check at the close of Week 7, before the project. Light skim, not deep feedback. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is being built steadily, so the project has something to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_GT_ReadingJournal_Module1). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • Mid-module check (around Week 4): your journal should be current through Week 4 (Part II opening).
  • End-of-module check (end of Week 7): your journal should be current through Week 7, with a project claim taking shape in Section 5.

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the text?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are the weeks up to date?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a claim forming, with at least one or two pieces of evidence attached (especially at the end-of-module check)?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | All required weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details. Section 5 shows a claim (end-of-module: claim plus evidence). | | Partial credit | Most weeks present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several weeks empty; little or no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points each check). Drop at most one brief public-style note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 3 before the project" or "Strong evidence in Section 5, keep going"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at each checkpoint. Two checkpoints in the module. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Friday Check-up.

You have now read both of Gulliver’s big voyages: tiny Lilliput, where he looms over a foolish little court, and giant Brobdingnag, where a wise king looks down on him. Week 6
Word Study: Words from the Country of the Houyhnhnms
Assignment · about 18 minutes · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
conjecture (to guess at something without proof): “...it was impossible for me to conjecture what it meant...” (Ch. 1)
antipathy (a strong, deep dislike): “...one against which I naturally conceived so strong an antipathy.” (Ch. 1)
abominable (causing disgust or hatred; truly hateful): “...when I observed in this abominable animal, a perfect human figure...” (Ch. 2)
avarice (extreme greed for wealth): “...from their natural bent either to profusion or avarice...” (Ch. 6)
benevolence (kindness; goodwill toward others): “Friendship and benevolence are the two principal virtues among the Houyhnhnms.” (Ch. 8)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
antipathy comes from the Greek roots anti-, meaning “against,” and path, meaning “feeling” (the same root in sympathy and empathy). Antipathy is a feeling directed against someone or something: a strong dislike.
abominable comes from the Latin roots ab-, meaning “away from,” and omin, meaning “omen” (the same root in ominous). Something abominable was originally treated as a bad omen to turn away from; now it simply means hateful.
benevolence comes from the Latin roots bene, meaning “well” or “good,” and vol, meaning “to wish” (the same root in volunteer). Benevolence is the wish to do well by others.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what avarice means in the line “from their natural bent either to profusion or avarice”? Think it through before you check the definition.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the vocabulary section of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “...the most pernicious race of little odious vermin...”
Your rewrite: “...the most harmful and hateful little creatures...”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the book.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words and meanings recorded in the Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Week 6 Word Study
Type your three rewrites and your own sentence in the submission box. Keep the word list in your Reading Journal.

Week 7
Word Study: Words from the Voyage Home
Assignment · about 18 minutes · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
expedient (a plan or method for getting something done): “...my master proposed an expedient to the assembly...” (Ch. 9)
tranquillity (a state of calm and peace): “I enjoyed perfect health of body, and tranquillity of mind...” (Ch. 10)
antipathy (a strong, settled dislike): “...I... strove to conceal my antipathy against human kind...” (Ch. 11)
veracity (truthfulness; the habit of telling the truth): “...at last began to have a better opinion of my veracity.” (Ch. 11)
magnanimous (noble and generous in spirit; big-hearted): “...instead of proposals for conquering that magnanimous nation...” (Ch. 12)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
expedient comes from the Latin roots ex-, meaning “out,” and ped, meaning “foot” (the same root in pedestrian). To expedite something is literally to free its feet so it can move quickly; an expedient is a quick, workable solution.
veracity comes from the Latin root ver, meaning “true” (the same root in verify and verdict). Veracity is a habit of speaking the truth.
magnanimous comes from the Latin roots magn, meaning “great,” and anim, meaning “spirit” or “mind” (the same roots in magnificent and animosity). A magnanimous person has a great, generous spirit.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES

Your rewrite: “...a higher opinion of how truthful I was.”

assignments.title: Reading Journal Check — End of Module (Week 7)
assignments.html:
# Reading Journal Check: Gulliver's Travels (Tier 2 checkpoints)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). Two occurrences per module: a mid-module check around Week 4 and an end-of-module check at the close of Week 7, before the project. Light skim, not deep feedback. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is being built steadily, so the project has something to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_GT_ReadingJournal_Module1). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • Mid-module check (around Week 4): your journal should be current through Week 4 (Part II opening).
  • End-of-module check (end of Week 7): your journal should be current through Week 7, with a project claim taking shape in Section 5.

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the text?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are the weeks up to date?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a claim forming, with at least one or two pieces of evidence attached (especially at the end-of-module check)?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | All required weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details. Section 5 shows a claim (end-of-module: claim plus evidence). | | Partial credit | Most weeks present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several weeks empty; little or no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points each check). Drop at most one brief public-style note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 3 before the project" or "Strong evidence in Section 5, keep going"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at each checkpoint. Two checkpoints in the module. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Friday Check-up.

assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online

7TH GRADE ENGLISH LANGUAGE ARTS
Quarter / Module

Gulliver’s Travels
Final Project
Part 1: Written Argument
Opens / Due
Opens Week 7 · Due Week 8
Submission
Word doc
Graded with rubric
FINAL PROJECT · PART 1 OF 2
Miniature Worlds and Giant Perspectives: Your Written Argument
Short argument · about 400 to 600 words · about 60 minutes of writing time, spread out
📖 WHAT YOU ARE WRITING ABOUT
Across his voyages, Gulliver is first a giant in Lilliput, then a tiny man in Brobdingnag, and finally an outsider among the Houyhnhnms. Each change in size and perspective shows Swift’s real subject: the folly of human pride. You have practiced this argument in Quick Writes 5, 6, and 7. Now you pull that work together into one clear written argument.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Which voyage best reveals Swift’s view of humanity and the folly of human pride, and how do you know?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write a short argument that answers the focus question. Pick the one voyage you think reveals the most about human pride, make a claim, support it with evidence from the book, explain how that evidence proves your point, and close with a conclusion. Build it from your Quick Write 5 to 7 work in your Reading Journal (Section 5). This is one half of your project; the creative and VR half is a separate assignment.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Make a claim. Choose the voyage (Lilliput, Brobdingnag, or the land of the Houyhnhnms) that you think best reveals Swift’s view of human pride. Write one sentence that states your answer to the focus question.
2
Give your evidence. Use two or three specific details or short quotations from that voyage. Cite each one in MLA format: Swift’s last name plus the part and chapter, for example (Swift, Part II, Ch. 5). If you already name Swift in your sentence, just give the part and chapter. Pull these from Section 5 of your Reading Journal.
3
Explain each piece. After each detail, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your claim about pride. Do not just drop the quotation; explain what it means.
4
Write a conclusion. End with two or three sentences that restate your claim in fresh words and say what Swift wants readers to see about themselves.
5
Add your Works Cited entry. At the end of your document, add one entry for the novel: Swift, Jonathan. Gulliver’s Travels. 1726.
6
Be honest about your reasoning. If a detail only partly fits, say so. Naming where your evidence is strong and where it is weaker makes your argument stronger, not weaker.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
A clear claim names one voyage and answers the focus question.
☐
Two or three pieces of evidence from the book, each cited in MLA format (author plus part and chapter).
☐
Each piece of evidence is explained, not just quoted.
☐
A conclusion ties the argument back to the theme of human pride.
☐
A Works Cited entry for the novel appears at the end of the document.
☐
Writing uses headings or paragraphs and is checked for clear sentences and spelling.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP
Before you submit, make sure you have:
☐ Written in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐ Named your file LastName_GT_FinalArgument (for example, Garcia_GT_FinalArgument).
☐ Set line spacing to double throughout the document.
☐ Added your name, the course, and the date in the upper left, then centered a real title above your writing (MLA-style heading).
☐ Used Heading styles for any section labels and a readable body font (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐ Saved it to your Optima > ELA > [your course folder] in OneDrive and confirmed it is there.
☐ Submitted through Canvas (your copy opens automatically, or use the OneDrive tab).
M365 Skill You’re Practicing: Applying Heading Styles (Word).
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: GT Final Project: Written Argument
Submit your Word document through Canvas. This argument and the creative plus VR half are graded together on one rubric.
Due: end of Week 8.
You already did the thinking in your Quick Writes. This is where it comes together.

Graded with rubric
FINAL PROJECT · PART 2 OF 2
Miniature Worlds and Giant Perspectives: Your Creative Contrast
Visual + VR scene + reflection · spread across the project window
🎨 WHAT YOU ARE MAKING
In Lilliput, Gulliver is the giant looking down on petty, self-important tiny people. In Brobdingnag, he is the tiny one, forced to see human flaws from below. You will show that contrast in two ways: a visual you create, and a VR scene that stages the size difference. Together they make the theme of human pride something a viewer can see and stand inside.
🖌 PART A: YOUR VISUAL CONTRAST (choose one)
Create one visual that places Lilliput and Brobdingnag side by side and shows the reversal of scale. Pick the format you like best:
●
A diorama built from materials at home, photographed.
●
Digital artwork made with any drawing or design tool.
●
A comic strip of three to six panels showing the same Gulliver in both worlds.
Whichever you choose, the size reversal must be obvious, and your visual must point at the theme: that a change in perspective exposes human pride.
🔮 PART B: YOUR VR CONTRAST SCENE
You have already staged both halves of this in VR: the tiny world of Lilliput in Week 1, and the giant world of Brobdingnag in Week 4. Now bring them together into one scene that a viewer can walk through and feel the reversal.
📝 IN YOUR VR SETTING, DO THIS
1
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like that gives you open ground and room to build two areas.
2
On one side, rebuild your Lilliput scene: a large shape for Gulliver among many tiny objects. On the other side, rebuild your Brobdingnag scene: a tiny shape for Gulliver among oversized objects.
3
Add two labels or sticky notes, one per side, each naming the detail your scene shows and how pride looks from that point of view.
4
Stand between the two and look from one side to the other. Then record a short video or take a screenshot inside VR that captures both sides. If VR is not available to you, you may write a short paragraph describing the scene you would build instead.
5
Add a spoken explanation, 30 to 60 seconds long: narrate what your scene shows, in order from the Lilliput side to the Brobdingnag side, and name the one key point it makes about human pride. Record this narration as part of your video, or as a short stand-alone audio or video clip if you captured a screenshot or wrote a description instead. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone; it does not trade off against a silent screenshot.
📝 PART C: YOUR REFLECTION (200 to 250 words)
Write a reflection of 200 to 250 words in Word. Explain what you learned about human pride from building this contrast. What did the change from giant to tiny show you that reading alone did not? How do the perspectives in Lilliput and Brobdingnag help you understand the theme?
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The visual shows both worlds and makes the size reversal obvious.
☐
The VR scene stages both sides with two labels and is captured as a video, screenshot, or written description.
☐
The reflection is 200 to 250 words and connects the contrast to the theme of human pride.
☐
All three parts are submitted together.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your reflection in Word, name it LastName_GT_ProjectReflection, and save it to your OneDrive course folder. Upload your visual (a photo or file) and your VR video or screenshot with it.
🧑‍🏫 FACILITATOR NOTE
This is the creative half of the module’s one graded project; grade it together with the written argument on the single project rubric. Students reuse the Week 1 and Week 4 VR scenes, so most have the raw material already. Accept a written description in place of a VR capture for any student without headset access, with no penalty.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: GT Final Project: Creative + VR
Upload three things: your visual, your VR video or screenshot (or written description), and your Word reflection.
Due: end of Week 8.
Optima Academy Online · 7TH GRADE ENGLISH LANGUAGE ARTS · Quarter 1 · Gulliver’s Travels
Final Project · Part 2: Creative + VR

# The Call of the Wild: Reading Journal / Module Organizer (M365 Word doc spec)

Module 2 instance, built from the course-shared TEMPLATE. This is the exact spec for the Word document each student copies at the start of Module 2 and keeps in the OneDrive course folder. Hand it out through the Canvas + OneDrive LTI assignment so each student gets their own copy. The five fixed sections match every module of the course.

Hard rules. No em dashes in student-facing text. Name craft terms plainly. Dates carry A.D. or B.C. where relevant.

---

## Document setup and layout

  • File type: Microsoft Word (.docx), from the student's school M365 account.
  • File name: LastName_CotW_ReadingJournal_Module2 (example: Garcia_CotW_ReadingJournal_Module2).
  • Save location: Optima > ELA > [Course_Semester] in OneDrive.
  • Font: Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12.
  • Headings: Word Heading 1 for each Section; Heading 2 for each week block in Section 3.
  • Page numbers: bottom of the page.

M365 Skill You're Practicing: Applying Heading Styles and Inserting a Table (Word).

---

## COVER (first page)

  • Course: 7th Grade English Language Arts
  • Module: Module 2, The Call of the Wild (Jack London, 1903)
  • Student name: [student types]
  • Module Question / Theme: What transforms Buck from a pampered house dog into a creature of the wild, and what does his change reveal about instinct, survival, and the pull between civilization and the wild?

Center the block; course name largest; module question in italics beneath.

---

## SECTION 1: Module Question (your evolving answer)

Heading 1: Section 1, Module Question

The big question for this module is below. You will answer it many times. Do not erase old answers. Add a new dated line each week so you can watch your thinking change.

Module Question: What transforms Buck from a pampered house dog into a creature of the wild, and what does his change reveal about instinct, survival, and the pull between civilization and the wild?

  • Week 1 answer (date): _______
  • Week 2 answer (date): _______
  • Week 3 answer (date): _______
  • Week 4 answer (date): _______
  • Week 5 answer (date): _______

---

## SECTION 2: Word Study

Heading 1: Section 2, Word Study

Each week you study a small set of words from the reading. Add every word to the table below. Write what it means in your own words, and copy the exact line from the book where you met it.

Insert one Word table with these exact headers, pre-loaded with a divider row per week and empty rows for each word:

| Word | What it means (in your own words) | The line it came from (with chapter) | |------|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|

Pre-load these week labels. The exact word list for each week is set in that week's Word Study lesson; where a week is not yet final, leave clearly marked blank rows. Starter words drawn from the reading are listed to show the level:

  • Week 1, Ch. 1 Into the Primitive: primitive, imperiously, demesne, primordial, lacerated (or words added in the Word Study lesson)
  • Week 2, Ch. 2 The Law of Club and Fang: retrogression, unwonted, vicarious, salient, obliterate (or words added in the Word Study lesson)
  • Week 3, Ch. 3 The Dominant Primordial Beast: dominant, primordial, antagonist, cunning, marauder (or words added in the Word Study lesson)
  • Week 4, Ch. 4 to 5 Who Has Won to Mastership; The Toil of Trace and Trail: obdurate, celerity, morose, callowness, slovenly (the confirmed list from the built Word Study lesson)

## SECTION 3: Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

Heading 1: Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses

This is the heart of your journal. There is one block per week. When a lesson says "Add this to the Week ___ section of your Reading Journal," this is where it goes. Each week block has two parts: the reading-response prompts (answer these in full sentences) and a space for your own notes.

Create one Heading 2 block per week, exactly as below. The authoritative prompts live in that week's reading lessons; paste each week's prompts here verbatim when the week is built. Until then, keep the labeled space and the reading so the student knows what is coming.

### Heading 2: Week 1, Ch. 1 Into the Primitive

How the setting changes from Santa Clara to the Northland, and how that change starts to change Buck.] 3. [From the Week 1 reading lessons. Buck's first lesson from the man with the club.]

## SECTION 4: Craft, Characters, Theme (running notes)

Heading 1: Section 4, Craft, Characters, Theme

Use this section all module long. When a lesson names a craft move (point of view, figurative language, tone, symbol) or you notice how Buck changes, add a short note here with the chapter. You will pull from this section when you build your project.

  • Craft moves I noticed: (term, what it was, the chapter)
  • Characters and how they change: (especially Buck, who is a different creature by the end of Chapter 7)
  • Theme ideas: (a big idea London seems to be building, and one detail that supports it)

---

## SECTION 5: Toward the Project (your developing argument)

Heading 1: Section 5, Toward the Project

Your module project is an argumentative essay. You make a claim and back it up. Build that argument here, a little at a time, using your Quick Writes (especially Quick Writes 2, 3, 4, and 5). By the end you should have a thesis, two or three pieces of evidence with explanation, a counterclaim with your response, and a conclusion idea.

  • The project question: Does Buck's transformation set him free, or destroy who he was? (Or: what does the novel argue about the call of the wild?)

## Reminder line for the bottom of the document

Keep this document in your OneDrive course folder all module long. Your teacher reviews Sections 2, 3, and 5 at the Reading Journal Check (around Week 3 and at the end of the module). You are not turning it in every week; you are building it every week.

Week 1
Word Study: Words from Into the Primitive
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
nomadic (wandering from place to place, with no settled home): “Old longings nomadic leap, chafing at custom’s chain.” (Ch. 1, the opening verse)
demesne (a piece of land that someone owns and rules): “And over this great demesne Buck ruled.” (Ch. 1)
treachery (a betrayal of trust): “...on the memorable night of Manuel’s treachery.” (Ch. 1)
primitive (belonging to the earliest, wildest stage; raw and uncivilized): “It was his introduction to the reign of primitive law.” (Ch. 1)
metamorphosed (changed completely into something different): “...he was metamorphosed into a raging fiend.” (Ch. 1)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
primitive comes from the Latin root prim-, meaning “first.” Something primitive belongs to the earliest, rawest stage of things, before it was refined or civilized.
metamorphosed comes from two Greek roots: meta- (“change”) and morph- (“form”). To be metamorphosed is to be changed completely from one form into another.
nomadic comes from the Greek root nomad-, from a word meaning “to roam in search of pasture.” A nomadic life is one spent wandering from place to place instead of settling down.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what demesne means? Think it through in your head or jot a note in your Reading Journal; you do not need to write this down for submission.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the vocabulary section of your Reading Journal, along with the line each word comes from.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “It was his introduction to the reign of primitive law.”
Your rewrite: “This was the first time he met the raw, lawless world of the wild.”
3
Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the book.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words, meanings, and source lines recorded in the Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Week 1 Word Study
Type your three rewrites and your own sentence in the submission box. Keep the word list in your Reading Journal.

VR Activity 1
Two Worlds: The Sunny Valley and the Frozen North
Solo VR activity · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
Buck’s transformation begins with a change of setting. In VR you will build the two worlds side by side: the warm, comfortable Santa Clara Valley where Buck was king, and the cold, harsh Northland he is dragged into. Standing between them, you will see what the new place takes from him. Save your work. It becomes raw material for your module project on Buck’s transformation.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · your copy of Chapter 1 (look back at the Santa Clara Valley pages and the kidnapping pages for details).
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual setting for this course. Choose any setting you like that gives you a wide open space you can divide in two. You only need room for a “warm” side and a “cold” side, with space to place objects and labels.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Build the warm side: Santa Clara Valley. Place objects that stand for Buck’s old life: the big house, the lawns, the swimming tank, a warm fire. This is where Buck was king.
2
Build the cold side: the Northland. Place objects that stand for the harsh new world: snow, a sled, a crate, a length of rope. This is where Buck must fight to live.
3
Add two labels or sticky notes, one per side. On the warm side, write one word for the Buck who lived there. On the cold side, write one word for the Buck the new place is making. Use words from the chapter if you can (for example, “king” and “fiend”).

Word Study: Words from the Law of Club and Fang
Assignment · 10 pts
⌚ ABOUT 18 MINUTES
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
primordial (belonging to the earliest, most ancient times; wild and primitive): “...flung into the heart of things primordial.”
vicarious (experienced through watching someone else rather than going through it yourself): “...it was a vicarious experience, else he would not have lived to profit by it.”
ignominiously (in a way that brings shame or disgrace): “...till he recovered from his consternation and fled ignominiously into the outer cold.”
fastidiousness (fussiness; the habit of being very picky): “He swiftly lost the fastidiousness which had characterized his old life.”
retrogression (a change backward to an earlier or lower state): “His development (or retrogression) was rapid.”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
primordial comes from two Latin roots: primus (“first”) and ordium (“beginning”). Something primordial belongs to the very first beginning of things, before it was developed.
vicarious comes from the Latin root vic-, from a word meaning “a turn, a substitute.” A vicarious experience is one you get by standing in another creature’s place, not by living through it yourself.
retrogression comes from the Latin prefix retro- (“backward”) joined to gress, a root meaning “to step.” Retrogression is a step backward to an earlier, less developed state.

Field Dispatch 1
MODULE 2 · THE CALL OF THE WILD · CH. 1 TO 2
25 points3 to 5 minDue end of Week 2
Dispatch from the Trail
A broadcast dispatch filed from where the events happened. The correspondent reads the scene from the page, then files the report.
FORMATFiled broadcast dispatch
VOICEOne correspondent. Yours.
DATELINEThe Northland trail, from the chapter you choose
Run sheet
 
SEGSEGMENTRUNS
01
Dateline
Name the book, the chapter, and where on the trail this happens. Say what has just happened.
:20 to :30
02
From the scene
Read the passage aloud, as written.
1:30 to 2:30
03
The filed report
One angle from the three below.
1:00 to 2:00

Sign-off
Close the dispatch. One sentence.
:10
TOTAL RUNTIME3 to 5 min
One recording. All four segments in order, no stopping between them.
01  Dateline
 
Open with this.
“Dispatch from the trail. This is ______, Chapter ______. Just before this, ______.”
Other wording is permitted if it carries the same facts.
02  From the scene
 
SOURCEChapters 1 and 2.
LENGTH350 to 550 words. Check the word count. Do not count by hand.
TEXTRead it as written. No summarising, no skipping, no paraphrase.
PREPTwo rehearsals. The first finds the words that trip you. The second decides where the sentences breathe.
NAMESUnfamiliar names are attempted out loud, not skipped.
Passages that carry aloud
›Ch. 1, the Santa Clara valley. The last calm writing in the book. Read it slowly, because nothing after it is slow.
›Ch. 1, the man in the red sweater. A lesson taught with a club, reported without comment.
›Ch. 1, the express car. Short sentences, rising. Easy to rush and worth not rushing.
›Ch. 2, the death of Curly. Thirty seconds of violence and a conclusion drawn from it.
›Ch. 2, the first night in the snow. A discovery scene. Quiet after Curly, and the contrast is the point.
The Call of the Wild is public domain and the full text is on the literature lesson pages. Read from the screen.
03  The filed report
 
Keep recording. Complete one of the three. They carry equal weight.
AWhat the scene shows1:00 TO 2:00
A correspondent reports what was observed, not what was felt about it. Cover any two.
›One thing this passage shows about Buck, or about the men, that was not clear before it.
›One word London chose here that a plainer word could not have done.
›What reading it aloud revealed that reading it silently did not.
›The question the scene leaves open.
BThe correspondent's verdict1:00 TO 2:00
File a verdict on something debatable in the passage just read. Take the side most listeners will not.
›Name the arguable thing: a choice someone makes, a line that reads two ways, or something London does that you judge a mistake.
›State your verdict in one sentence. If nobody could disagree with it, it is not a verdict yet.
›Quote the words. You have just read them.
›Answer the strongest objection to your verdict.
CThe dispatch that was not filed1:00 TO 2:00
Alter one moment inside the passage and report the consequence.
›Name the exact sentence being changed.
›State what happens instead.
›State what London's version does that yours does not. Then say which one you prefer, and why.
Delivery
 
RECORDERRecord / Upload Media records straight into Canvas.
ALTERNATERecord on a phone and upload the file.
TRACKAudio only is a complete submission. Video is permitted, never required.
ATTEMPTSTwo.
CONTINUITYOne take, all four segments, in order, no stopping between them.
Specification met when
 
☐Segment 01 names the source and the moment.
☐The passage is read aloud, in full, as written.
☐One angle is completed after the reading.
☐The angle points at a specific line, not at the story in general.
☐Played back once. Audible the whole way through.

📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
primordial (belonging to the earliest, most ancient stage; primitive): “The dominant primordial beast was strong in Buck.”
deliberateness (acting in a slow, careful, unhurried way): “A certain deliberateness characterized his attitude.”
supremacy (the position of highest power or authority): “the thing which projected their struggle for supremacy far into the future.”
pandemonium (wild, noisy disorder; uproar): “a shrill yelp of pain, heralded the breaking forth of pandemonium.”
inexorable (impossible to stop or change; relentless): “There was no hope for him. Buck was inexorable.”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
deliberateness comes from the Latin prefix de- joined to libr-, the root of the word for “a scale.” To act with deliberateness is to move as carefully as someone weighing something out on a scale.
pandemonium comes from two Greek roots: pan- (“all”) and daimon (“spirit”). It was first used for the capital of Hell in a poem, a place of all the demons, and now means a wild, noisy disorder.
inexorable comes from the Latin prefix in- (“not”) joined to a root meaning “to beg or pray.” Something inexorable cannot be turned aside no matter how much you plead with it.

assignments.title: Reading Journal Check — Mid-Module (Week 3)
assignments.html:
# Reading Journal Check: The Call of the Wild (Tier 2 checkpoints)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). Two occurrences per module: a mid-module check around Week 3 and an end-of-module check at the close of Week 5, before the project. Light skim, not deep feedback. Metadata: Q2 / Module 2. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is being built steadily, so the project has something to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_CotW_ReadingJournal_Module2). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • Mid-module check (around Week 3): your journal should be current through Week 3 (Buck versus Spitz, the primordial beast).
  • End-of-module check (end of Week 5): your journal should be current through Week 5 (John Thornton and the poem), with a project argument taking shape in Section 5 (a thesis and at least one or two pieces of evidence).

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the text?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are the weeks up to date?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a thesis forming, with at least one or two pieces of evidence and explanation attached (especially at the end-of-module check)? Is a counterclaim starting to appear?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | All required weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details. Section 5 shows a thesis (end-of-module: thesis plus evidence and a starting counterclaim). | | Partial credit | Most weeks present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several weeks empty; little or no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points each check). Drop at most one brief public-style note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 2 before the project" or "Strong thesis in Section 5, keep adding evidence"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at each checkpoint. Two checkpoints in the module. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Friday Check-up.

Word Study: Words from the Trail and the Camp
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
obdurate (stubborn; refusing to give in): “François was obdurate, but when he turned his back Buck again displaced Sol-leks.” (Ch. 4)
celerity (great speed; swiftness): “...the celerity with which Buck broke them in took away François’s breath.” (Ch. 4)
morose (gloomy and ill-tempered): “He became more morose and irritable...” (Ch. 4, about Dave)
callowness (lack of experience; immaturity): “It advertised his callowness, a callowness sheer and unutterable.” (Ch. 5, about Hal)
slovenly (messy, careless, and disorderly): “...the sled loaded in fashion so slovenly...” (Ch. 5, about Hal, Charles, and Mercedes)
🌱 WORD ROOTS
obdurate comes from the Latin prefix ob- (“against”) joined to durare, a root meaning “to harden” (from durus, “hard”). Someone obdurate has hardened themselves against giving in.
celerity comes from the Latin root celer, meaning “swift.” The same root gives us the word “accelerate.” Celerity means great speed.
morose comes from the Latin root mor-, from a word for a person’s settled mood or manner. Someone morose is stuck in a gloomy, ill-tempered mood.
🔍 BEFORE YOU'RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what slovenly means? Think it through in your head or jot a note in your Reading Journal; you do not need to write this down for submission.

Original: “He became more morose and irritable...”

Then write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the book.

🎯 THE IDEA

Week 5
Word Study: Words from “For the Love of a Man”
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK'S WORDS (with the line they come from)
convalescence (the time of recovering health after illness or injury): “...Buck romped through his convalescence and into a new existence.”
demonstrative (openly showing feelings): “Nig, equally friendly, though less demonstrative...”
ministrations (acts of care or service given to someone): “...till he came to look for her ministrations as much as he did for Thornton’s.”
primordial (belonging to the earliest, most ancient times): “Mercy did not exist in the primordial life.”
peremptorily (in a way that demands obedience and allows no refusal): “So peremptorily did these shades beckon him...”
🌱 WORD ROOTS
convalescence comes from the Latin prefix con- joined to valescere, a root meaning “to grow strong” (from valere, “to be well”). Convalescence is the time spent growing strong and well again after being sick or hurt.
demonstrative comes from the Latin root monstr-, meaning “to show.” Someone demonstrative shows their feelings openly instead of keeping them hidden.
peremptorily comes from the Latin prefix per- (“thoroughly”) joined to a root meaning “to take.” Together they once meant “to decide finally, cutting off any argument,” which is why peremptorily describes a command that allows no refusal.

Your Essay Outline and Opening Paragraph
Composition · project feeder · 15 pts
🎯 THE IDEA
You have built every part of an argument over the last three weeks: a thesis, a piece of evidence with explanation, and a counterclaim with a conclusion. This week you pull them together. You will lay out the full outline for your argumentative essay and write a draft introduction. This becomes the spine of your final project, so do it carefully.
❓ YOUR ESSAY QUESTION
Does Buck’s transformation set him free, or does it destroy who he was? (Or take up the related question: what does the novel argue about the call of the wild?)
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Build your outline. Open Quick Writes 2, 3, and 4, and arrange their parts into this order. Write each part as a short heading with a sentence or two underneath:
• Introduction and thesis (your claim, from Quick Write 2)
• Body 1: evidence and explanation (your quote plus reasoning, from Quick Write 3)
• Body 2: counterclaim and response (the other side and your answer, from Quick Write 4)

# Reading Journal Check: The Call of the Wild (Tier 2 checkpoints)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). Two occurrences per module: a mid-module check around Week 3 and an end-of-module check at the close of Week 5, before the project. Light skim, not deep feedback. Metadata: Q2 / Module 2. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is being built steadily, so the project has something to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_CotW_ReadingJournal_Module2). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • Mid-module check (around Week 3): your journal should be current through Week 3 (Buck versus Spitz, the primordial beast).
  • End-of-module check (end of Week 5): your journal should be current through Week 5 (John Thornton and the poem), with a project argument taking shape in Section 5 (a thesis and at least one or two pieces of evidence).

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are the weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the text?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are the weeks up to date?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a thesis forming, with at least one or two pieces of evidence and explanation attached (especially at the end-of-module check)? Is a counterclaim starting to appear?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | All required weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details. Section 5 shows a thesis (end-of-module: thesis plus evidence and a starting counterclaim). | | Partial credit | Most weeks present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; several weeks empty; little or no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points each check). Drop at most one brief public-style note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 2 before the project" or "Strong thesis in Section 5, keep adding evidence"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at each checkpoint. Two checkpoints in the module. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Friday Check-up.

FINAL PROJECT · PART 1 OF 2
The Call of the Wild: Your Argumentative Essay
Argumentative essay · about 500 to 700 words · about 70 minutes of writing time, spread out
📖 WHAT YOU ARE WRITING ABOUT
Buck begins as the king of a warm, comfortable home and ends as a creature of the wild, running with the wolves. Readers disagree about what that change means. Some say the wild sets Buck free to become what he truly is. Others say it destroys the loyal, loving dog he once was. You have practiced this argument in Quick Writes 2, 3, 4, and 5: a thesis, evidence with explanation, and a counterclaim. Now you pull that work together into one clear argumentative essay.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Does Buck’s transformation set him free, or destroy who he was?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write an argumentative essay that answers the focus question. Take a clear position, state it as a thesis, support it with evidence from the book and explain that evidence, raise the strongest argument against your view and answer it, then close with a conclusion. Build it from your Quick Write 2 to 5 work in your Reading Journal (Section 5). This is one half of your project; the creative and VR half is a separate assignment.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Write your thesis. Decide your position on the focus question: does the change set Buck free, or destroy who he was? Write one clear sentence that states your answer. This is your thesis. Put it at the end of a short opening paragraph that sets up the question.
2
Give your evidence and explain it. Use two or three specific details or short quotations from the book that support your thesis. Cite each one in MLA format: London’s last name plus the chapter, for example (London, Ch. 3). If you already name London in your sentence, just give the chapter. After each one, write a sentence or two that shows how it proves your point. Do not just drop the quotation; explain what it means. Pull these from Section 5 of your Reading Journal.
3
Raise a counterclaim and answer it. Name the strongest argument someone on the other side would make. For example, if you argue the wild sets Buck free, a reader might point to how much he loves John Thornton. State that fairly in a sentence or two, then explain why your position still holds.
4
Write a conclusion. End with two or three sentences that restate your thesis in fresh words and say what London wants readers to understand about instinct, survival, and the pull between civilization and the wild.
5
Add your Works Cited entry. At the end of your document, add one entry for the novel: London, Jack. The Call of the Wild. 1903.
6
Be honest about your reasoning. If a detail only partly fits, say so. Taking the other side seriously in your counterclaim makes your argument stronger, not weaker.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
A clear thesis takes a position and answers the focus question.
☐
Two or three pieces of evidence from the book, each cited in MLA format (author plus chapter).
☐
Each piece of evidence is explained, not just quoted.
☐
A counterclaim is raised fairly and answered.
☐
A conclusion ties the argument back to the theme of civilization and the wild.
☐
A Works Cited entry for the novel appears at the end of the document.
☐
Writing uses clear paragraphs and is checked for clear sentences and spelling.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP
Before you submit, make sure you have:
☐ Written in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐ Named your file LastName_CotW_FinalEssay (for example, Garcia_CotW_FinalEssay).
☐ Set line spacing to double throughout the document.
☐ Added your name, the course, and the date in the upper left, then centered a real title above your writing (MLA-style heading).
☐ Used Heading styles for any section labels and a readable body font (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐ Saved it to your Optima > ELA > [your course folder] in OneDrive and confirmed it is there.
☐ Submitted through Canvas (your copy opens automatically, or use the OneDrive tab).
M365 Skill You’re Practicing: Applying Heading Styles (Word).

Canvas Assignment Name: CotW Final Project: Argumentative Essay
Submit your Word document through Canvas. This essay and the creative plus VR half are graded together on one rubric.
Due: end of Week 6.
You already did the thinking in your Quick Writes. This is where it comes together.

FINAL PROJECT · PART 2 OF 2
The Call of the Wild: Your Transformation Piece
Visual + VR scene + reflection · spread across the project window
🎨 WHAT YOU ARE MAKING
Buck starts as a pampered house dog in the sunny Santa Clara Valley and ends as a creature of the wild. You will show that transformation in two ways: a visual you create, and a VR scene that a viewer can stand inside. Together they make Buck’s change from civilization to the wild something a viewer can see and feel.
🖌 PART A: YOUR TRANSFORMATION VISUAL (choose one)
Create one visual that shows Buck’s transformation from the tame house dog to the creature of the wild. Pick the format you like best:
●
A "before and after" art piece, drawn by hand or made with any digital tool, showing Buck at Judge Miller’s place beside Buck in the wild.
●
A comic strip of three to six panels that shows the key moments of Buck’s change.
●
A map of Buck’s journey from the Santa Clara Valley to the Northland, marking the places where he changes the most.
Whichever you choose, the transformation must be obvious, and your visual must point at the theme: that Buck is pulled between civilization and the wild, and the wild wins.
🔮 PART B: YOUR VR TRANSFORMATION SCENE
You have already staged both halves of this in VR: Buck’s old world and the Northland in Week 1, and a contrast scene in Week 4. Now bring them together into one scene that a viewer can walk through and feel the change from tame to wild.
📝 IN YOUR VR SETTING, DO THIS
1
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like that gives you open ground and room to build two areas.
2
On one side, rebuild Buck’s tame world: warm, comfortable, civilized, with objects that suggest the big house and easy living. On the other side, rebuild the wild: cold, open, and harsh, with objects that suggest the Northland and survival.
3
Add two labels or sticky notes, one per side, each naming the detail your scene shows and what it reveals about Buck at that point in his change.
4
Stand between the two sides and look from one to the other. Then record a short video or take a screenshot inside VR that captures both sides. If VR is not available to you, you may write a short paragraph describing the scene you would build instead.
5
Add a spoken explanation, 30 to 60 seconds long: narrate what your scene shows, in order from Buck’s tame world to the wild, and name the one key point it makes about the pull between civilization and the wild. Record this narration as part of your video, or as a short stand-alone audio or video clip if you captured a screenshot or wrote a description instead. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone; it does not trade off against a silent screenshot.
📝 PART C: YOUR REFLECTION (200 to 250 words)
Write a reflection of 200 to 250 words in Word. Explain what you learned about Buck’s transformation from building this contrast. What did standing between the tame world and the wild show you that reading alone did not? How do the two sides help you understand the pull between civilization and the wild, and your answer to the focus question?
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The visual shows both Buck’s tame world and the wild and makes the transformation obvious.
☐
The VR scene stages both sides with two labels and is captured as a video, screenshot, or written description.
☐
The reflection is 200 to 250 words and connects the contrast to the theme of civilization and the wild.
☐
All three parts are submitted together.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your reflection in Word, name it LastName_CotW_ProjectReflection, and save it to your OneDrive course folder. Upload your visual (a photo or file) and your VR video or screenshot with it.
🧑‍🏫 FACILITATOR NOTE
This is the creative half of the module’s one graded project; grade it together with the argumentative essay on the single project rubric. Students reuse the Week 1 and Week 4 VR scenes, so most have the raw material already. Accept a written description in place of a VR capture for any student without headset access, with no penalty.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: CotW Final Project: Creative + VR
Upload three things: your visual, your VR video or screenshot (or written description), and your Word reflection.
Due: end of Week 6.
