Week 1
Word Study: Words from Staves 1 and 2
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 THIS WEEK’S WORDS (with the line they come from)
solitary (alone, isolated): “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.” (Stave 2)
avarice (extreme greed for money): “...the master-passion, Gain, engrossed his thoughts” — the Spirit shows Scrooge his own years of avarice. (Stave 2)
morose (gloomy, bad-tempered): “He was not the dogged, morose Scrooge...” (context: the young Scrooge before greed hardened him). (Stave 2)
penitence (sorrow and regret for wrongdoing): Marley’s ghost says he must do “incessant torture of remorse” for his lack of penitence in life. (Stave 1)
spectre (a ghost): “The spectre’s voice disturbed the very marrow in his bones.” (Stave 1)
🌟 WORD ROOTS
solitary comes from the Latin root sol, meaning “alone.” A solitary child is a child left alone, which is exactly how Dickens uses the word for the young Scrooge.
penitence comes from the Latin root poen (as in poena, “penalty”). The same root shows up in “penalty” and “penitentiary.” Feeling penitence means feeling the weight of a wrong almost like a punishment you give yourself.
spectre comes from the Latin root spect, meaning “to look” or “to see.” You can hear the same root in “spectacle,” “inspect,” and “spectator.” A spectre is literally something that appears to be seen.
💡 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what avarice means? Notice what Dickens says is driving all of Scrooge’s thoughts in that scene.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the Word Study section of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each, take the line it comes from and rewrite that line in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model using a different word:
Original: “The spectre’s voice disturbed the very marrow in his bones.”
Your rewrite: “The ghost’s voice shook him all the way to his deepest core.”
3
Write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. The sentence should connect to something that happens in Staves 1 or 2.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words and meanings recorded in the Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and use clear, correct wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly and connects to Staves 1 or 2.

Type your three rewrites and your own sentence in the submission box. Keep the full word list in your Reading Journal.

VR Activity 1
Forged in Iron: Staging Marley’s Chains and the Counting-House
Solo VR activity · about 25 minutes · 10 pts
🔮 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
Marley’s ghost drags a chain “made of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses wrought in steel.” In VR you can place those objects and feel what that chain looks like in three dimensions. You will also stage the cold, isolated counting-house that Dickens describes in Stave 1. Your arrangement and reflection become raw material for your book cover project.
📋 WHAT YOU WILL NEED
Your VR headset · about 25 minutes · a clear memory of Stave 1 (you may want to reread Marley’s description before you start).
📍 HOW TO ENTER
Put on your VR headset and open the class virtual space for this course. Choose any setting you like for an indoor space or a dim, enclosed environment. You want something that feels cold and confined, like a Victorian office or a dark interior space.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Place objects to represent the counting-house. Use a desk or table shape, a small light source or candle, and a locked box or container to stand for Scrooge’s coal box. Make the space feel small and cold.
2
Build Marley’s chain. Use any available objects (boxes, crates, padlock shapes, book-like objects, bags or pouches) to lay out a chain of objects on the ground. Try to arrange at least five or six linked items. The chain should be long.
3
Add two text labels. On one, write what each object in the chain represents from Dickens’s description (for example: “cash-box = a greedy choice”). On the second, write one word that describes what the whole scene makes you think about Scrooge’s future.
4
Stand beside the chain and look at the counting-house together. This is the world Scrooge built. Take a moment to notice how the two things relate before you capture your submission.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Take a screenshot inside VR (or record a short video, 30 to 60 seconds) showing the chain arrangement and your two labels, and upload it to Canvas. Then type two or three sentences: what did building the chain help you understand about Marley’s warning to Scrooge?

Week 2
Word Study: Words from the Final Staves
Assignment · 10 pts
📚 THIS WEEK’S WORDS (with the lines they come from)
benevolence (goodwill and generosity toward others): “the shopkeepers’ benevolence to dangle from conspicuous hooks, that people’s mouths might water gratis as they passed” (Stave 3)
penitence (deep sorrow and regret for doing wrong): “Scrooge hung his head to hear his own words quoted by the Spirit, and was overcome with penitence and grief.” (Stave 3)
phantom (a ghost or spirit; an apparition): “a solemn Phantom, draped and hooded, coming, like a mist along the ground, towards him.” (Stave 3/4)
avarice (extreme greed for wealth): “if this man could be raised up now, what would be his foremost thoughts? Avarice, hard-dealing, griping cares?” (Stave 4)
munificence (great generosity): “I don’t know what to say to such munifi—” (Stave 5 — the portly gentleman cannot finish the word when Scrooge pledges his back-payments)
🌟 WORD ROOTS
benevolence comes from two Latin parts: bene, meaning “well” or “good,” and vol, from velle, “to wish.” Put together they mean wishing someone well, which is exactly what benevolence is.
phantom comes from the Greek root phan, meaning “to show” or “to appear.” The same root shows up in “fantasy” and “phenomenon.” A phantom is something that appears, often where nothing solid should be.
munificence comes from the Latin munus, meaning “gift,” joined with a form of facere, “to make.” Munificence is, literally, gift-making: generosity on a grand scale.
💡 BEFORE YOU’RE TOLD: CONTEXT CLUES
Before you look at the meaning above, what in the surrounding words hints at what avarice means? Pay attention to the other words paired with it in that same sentence.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Add all five words and their meanings to the Word Study table in Section 2 of your Reading Journal.
2
Pick three of the words. For each one, take the sentence it comes from and rewrite it in your own words, keeping the meaning but changing the wording. Here is a model with a different word:
Original: “Scrooge hung his head to hear his own words quoted by the Spirit, and was overcome with penitence and grief.”
Your rewrite: “Scrooge bowed his head when he recognized his own cruel words coming from the Spirit. He felt a deep sorrow for what he had said.”
3
Write one new sentence of your own using any one of the five words correctly. It does not have to be about the book.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five words and meanings recorded in the Reading Journal.
☐
Three rewrites keep the original meaning and change the wording.
☐
Your own sentence uses the word correctly.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Week 2 Word Study
Type your three rewrites and your own sentence in the submission box. Keep the full word list in your Reading Journal.

📖 WHAT YOU ARE DOING
In Stave 5, Scrooge wakes from his last encounter with the Spirits and immediately begins acting on his transformation. In this VR activity, you will set the scene for that transformation: you will build a virtual space that contrasts who Scrooge was at the start of the novella with who he becomes by the end of Stave 5. Your VR headset

About 25 minutes

📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Build a “Before” area.
Arrange objects or labels to represent Scrooge at the start of the story. Use words like “cold,” “dark,” and “alone.” You might represent his counting-house, his solitary habits, or his refusal to give.

Build an “After” area nearby.

assignments.title: Reading Journal Check — End of Module (Week 2)
assignments.html:
# Reading Journal Check: A Christmas Carol (Tier 2 checkpoint)

Build in: Canvas Assignment (file/OneDrive submission of the student's Reading Journal Word doc, or a "mark as done" completion submission). No custom code; Canvas-native. Tier: 2 (community / light). One occurrence per module: an end-of-module check at the close of Week 2, before the project is submitted. Light skim, not deep feedback. Metadata: Q2 / Module 3. Purpose: confirm the Reading Journal is built through both weeks and that the project reflection has a starting claim with evidence, so the final project has something solid to stand on. The journal is NOT collected weekly; this is the only deeper review.

No em dashes. This is a light-touch review. Do not write per-prompt feedback; score on completion and drop a one-line note where useful.

---

## What the student does

Share or upload your Reading Journal Word doc from your OneDrive course folder (LastName_ACC_ReadingJournal_Module3). You are not rewriting anything. You are showing your steady work so far.

  • End-of-module check (end of Week 2): your journal should be current through Week 2 (all five staves), with a theme claim and at least two pieces of evidence taking shape in Section 5.

---

## What the teacher reviews (Sections 2, 3, and 5 only)

Skim three sections. Do not read every line.

  • Section 2, Word Study: Are both weeks' words present, with student-worded meanings and a line from the text?
  • Section 3, Weekly Reading Notes and Responses: Are the weekly prompts answered in full sentences, using details from the reading? Are Weeks 1 and 2 both present?
  • Section 5, Toward the Project: Is a theme claim forming, with at least one or two pieces of evidence attached? Is there a starting book-cover idea?

Ignore Sections 1 and 4 for scoring; they are the student's private working space.

---

## Completion rubric (simple, light)

| Rating | What it looks like | |--------|--------------------| | Full credit | Both weeks present in Sections 2 and 3. Prompts answered in full sentences with text details. Section 5 shows a theme claim with at least two pieces of evidence and a book-cover idea. | | Partial credit | One week mostly present but some prompts are blank, one-word, or missing text details; Section 5 thin or just started. | | Minimal credit | Large gaps; a whole week empty; no Section 5 work. |

Suggested points: small completion value (for example, 10 points). Drop at most one brief note per student where it helps (for example, "Catch up Week 1 prompts before you finish the project" or "Strong theme claim in Section 5, keep adding evidence"). No paragraph feedback.

---

## Teacher time note

Across 500 students this is a fast skim: roughly 30 to 45 seconds per journal at this single checkpoint. This is the deeper-review layer that lets weekly reading accountability stay on the auto-graded Friday Check-up.

assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
7TH GRADE ENGLISH LANGUAGE ARTS
Quarter / Module
Q2 · Module 3
A Christmas Carol
Final Project
Book Cover + Reflection + VR
Opens / Due
Opens Week 2 · Due end of Week 2
Submission
Cover + VR + reflection
Graded with rubric
FINAL PROJECT
A Christmas Carol: Your Book Cover + Reflection
Book cover (your choice of medium) + VR scene + 200 to 300 word written reflection · spread across the project window
🎨 WHAT YOU ARE MAKING
Scrooge begins the novella as a man who has shut out every human connection, and ends it as someone changed almost beyond recognition. You will capture that change, and the theme behind it, in three connected pieces: a book cover, a VR scene, and a written reflection. Together, they show that you have understood not just what happened in the story, but what it means.
🖌 PART A: YOUR BOOK COVER (choose your medium)
Design a book cover for A Christmas Carol that captures the novella’s central theme. A strong cover does not just illustrate a scene; it uses an image, a color, a symbol, or a composition to say something about what the story is really about. Pick the format you like best:
●
A hand-drawn cover, scanned or photographed.
●
A digital cover made in any design or drawing tool (including Microsoft Word or PowerPoint).
●
A collage of images, textures, or colors, assembled by hand or digitally.
Whatever you choose, the cover must include: (1) the title and author’s name placed somewhere on the design; (2) at least one image or symbol that points to the central theme; (3) a color or composition choice that fits the mood of the novella. The theme must be readable from the cover alone, without the reflection to explain it.
🔮 PART B: YOUR VR TRANSFORMATION SCENE
You have already built VR scenes this module that stage moments from the novella. Now use that work to set up one scene that captures Scrooge’s transformation. A viewer standing in this scene should be able to feel the difference between who Scrooge was and who he becomes.
📝 IN YOUR VR SETTING, DO THIS
1
Put on your VR headset and open the virtual environment. Choose any setting you like that gives you enough space to arrange two areas side by side.
2
On one side, place objects or labels that represent Scrooge before: cold, isolated, defined by money and self-interest. On the other side, place objects or labels that represent Scrooge after: open, generous, reconnected to the people around him.
3
Add two labels or sticky notes, one per side: each should name one thing your scene shows and connect it to the theme you identified in the novella.
4
Record a short video or take a screenshot inside VR that shows both sides of your scene. If VR is not available to you, write a short paragraph (three to five sentences) describing the scene you would build instead. There is no penalty for using the written description.
5
Add a spoken explanation, 30 to 60 seconds long: narrate what your scene shows, in order from Scrooge before to Scrooge after, and name the one key point it makes about what changes him. Record this narration as part of your video, or as a short stand-alone audio or video clip if you captured a screenshot or wrote a description instead. This spoken part is required and graded for everyone; it does not trade off against a silent screenshot.
📝 PART C: YOUR WRITTEN REFLECTION (200 to 300 words)
Write a reflection of 200 to 300 words in Word. Your reflection has two jobs:
●
Explain your book cover. What image or symbol did you choose, and why does it capture the central theme? Point to at least one specific detail from the novella, cited in MLA format: Dickens’s last name plus the stave, for example (Dickens, Stave 2). If you already name Dickens in your sentence, just give the stave.
●
Answer the module question. In your own words, what changes Scrooge: fear, memory, or love? Defend your answer with at least one moment from the text, cited the same way. If you think more than one force is at work, you can say so, but be specific about which does the most.
●
Add your Works Cited entry. At the end of your reflection, add one entry for the novella: Dickens, Charles. A Christmas Carol. 1843.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The book cover includes the title, the author’s name, at least one thematic image or symbol, and a color or composition choice that fits the novella’s mood.
☐
The VR scene stages Scrooge before and after, with two labels, and is captured as a video, screenshot, or written description.
☐
The reflection is 200 to 300 words, explains the cover choices with at least one text detail cited in MLA format (author plus stave), and answers the module question with cited evidence.
☐
A Works Cited entry for the novella appears at the end of the reflection.
☐
All three parts are submitted together.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP
Before you submit, make sure you have:
☐ Written your reflection in Microsoft Word, opened from your school M365 account.
☐ Named your reflection file LastName_ACC_ProjectReflection (for example, Garcia_ACC_ProjectReflection).
☐ Set line spacing to double throughout the document.
☐ Added your name, the course, and the date in the upper left, then centered a real title above your writing (MLA-style heading).
☐ Used a readable body font (Calibri 11 or Times New Roman 12).
☐ Saved it to your Optima > ELA > [your course folder] in OneDrive and confirmed it is there.
☐ If your book cover is digital, saved it as a file you can upload (a Word file, PowerPoint file, image, or PDF).
☐ Submitted through Canvas (OneDrive tab or direct upload).

This is the module’s one graded project; grade it on the single four-criterion rubric. Students have built VR scenes in Weeks 1 and 2 that give them raw material for Part B. The book cover may arrive as a photo, scan, Word file, PowerPoint slide, image file, or PDF; all formats are equally valid. Grade on how well the cover communicates the theme, not on artistic polish.

quizzes.title: Module 1 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description: Welcome to Module 1. You will read parts of Gulliver's Travels by Jonathan Swift, a famous voyage story that is really about people. Before you begin, answer a few quick questions. There are no wrong answers here. Your first thoughts give your teacher a starting point.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **How does changing your perspective change what you see, in others and in yourself?

In two or three sentences, give your first answer. You will come back to this question many times, so just say what you think right now.

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. By the end of this module you will be able to:

- [ ] Read and follow the events of Gulliver's voyages to Lilliput, Brobdingnag, and the land of the Houyhnhnms. - [ ] Explain how Swift uses exaggeration to make a point about people (this is called satire). - [ ] Track how a change in size and point of view changes what Gulliver sees. - [ ] Build one Reading Journal all module long and use it to grow a project claim. - [ ] Write a short argument and create a visual that shows the theme of human pride.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
One thing you are curious about. Name one thing about a voyage story, about tiny or giant people, or about this book that you are curious to find out. One sentence is fine.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal.)

A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea. Which word in this sentence is a noun?

"My father had a small estate in Nottinghamshire."

answers.text: had
small
estate
in

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. An estate is a thing you can own, so it is a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that names a person, place, thing, or idea. Try the "the ___" test.

questions.text: Which of these is a PROPER noun?

answers.text: Lilliput
country
people
island

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Lilliput is the name of one specific place, so it is capitalized.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names a specific person or place and starts with a capital letter.

questions.text: Which sentence contains an IDEA noun (a noun you cannot touch)?

answers.text: Gulliver ate the meat and bread.
The arrows landed on his hand.
The Lilliputians showed great courage near the giant.
He slept on the soft grass.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Courage is an idea. You cannot touch it, but it is still a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The other choices name things you can see or touch. Find the word that names a quality or idea.

questions.text: In the phrase "a small estate," what part of speech is the word "a"?

answers.text: a noun
a verb
an adjective that describes size
an article adjective

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The words a, an, and the are article adjectives. They sit in front of a noun and point to it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The words a, an, and the have their own name. They are article adjectives that point to the noun that follows.

questions.text:
A verb shows an action or a state of being. Which word in this sentence is the verb?

"I swam as fortune directed me."

answers.text: fortune
swam
me
as

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Swam shows what the subject does, so it is the verb. It is an action verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask what is being said about the subject. The word that shows what the subject does is the verb.

questions.text: Which of these is a LINKING verb (a verb that shows a state of being)?

answers.text: roared
climbed
pushed
was

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Was shows a state of being and links the subject to a description. It does not show an action.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Three of these are action verbs. A linking verb like is, am, are, was, or were shows a state of being.

questions.text:
In the verb phrase "was pushed," which word is the HELPING verb?

"He was pushed forward by wind and tide."

answers.text: was
pushed
forward
wind

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Was is the helping verb, and pushed is the main verb. The helping verb comes first.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In a verb phrase, the last verb is the main verb. The verb in front of it that helps it is the helping verb.

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence is NOT a noun and NOT a verb?

"The ingenious people quickly slung up a hogshead."

answers.text: people
slung
hogshead
quickly

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Quickly tells how the action happened, so it is an adverb, not a noun or a verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: People and hogshead name things, and slung names an action. One word only describes how the action happened.

questions.text: Who wrote Gulliver's Travels, and roughly when?

answers.text: Charles Dickens, 1840s
Jonathan Swift, 1720s
Jack London, 1900s
S. E. Hinton, 1960s

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Swift published it in 1726.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Those are other authors you will meet later this year. The author of Lilliput is Jonathan Swift.

questions.text: Satire is best defined as:

answers.text: A long poem about heroes.
A true story about a real voyage.
Using humor and exaggeration to criticize people or ideas.
A list of difficult vocabulary words.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Satire makes a serious point by exaggerating.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the satire visual in Lesson 1.01: exaggerate, hold up a mirror, make a point.

questions.text: How does Gulliver first arrive in Lilliput?

answers.text: He is invited by the emperor.
His ship is wrecked in a storm and he swims to shore.
He is born there.
He flies in a hot air balloon.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Antelope is wrecked, and Gulliver swims to the island.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the start of Chapter 1, after the storm.

questions.text: When Gulliver wakes on the beach, what has happened to him?

answers.text: He has been crowned king.
He is alone and free to explore.
Tiny people have tied him to the ground.
He has lost his memory.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The Lilliputians have staked him down with hundreds of tiny strings.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the moment Gulliver tries to stand up.

questions.text: In Chapter 2, the elaborate way the Lilliputians govern themselves is an example of Swift:

answers.text: describing a real country he visited.
gently mocking the pride and fuss of real governments.
explaining how to build a ship.
teaching a science lesson.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Swift shrinks a government to thumb size to question how seriously rulers take themselves.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember that the tiny, very serious government is satire of real politics.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a NOUN? "The ingenious people slung up a hogshead."

answers.text: ingenious
slung
people
up

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. People names a group, so it is a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "who or what?" to find the noun.

questions.text: Which is a PROPER noun?

answers.text: emperor
island
ship
Lilliput

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Lilliput is the specific name of a place, so it is capitalized.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names a specific person or place and starts with a capital letter.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is the VERB? "Gulliver swam toward the shore."

answers.text: Gulliver
swam
shore
toward

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Swam shows what the subject does, so it is the verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what is being said about the subject?" The answer is the verb.

questions.text:
An adjective describes a noun. Which word is the adjective in this sentence?

"The rope-dancers performed upon a slender thread."

answers.text: performed
slender
thread
upon

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Slender tells what kind of thread, so it is an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what kind, which one, or how many" about the noun thread. The answer is the adjective.

questions.text: Which set of questions does an adjective answer?

answers.text: How? When? Where?
Who owns it?
What kind? Which one? How many?
To what extent?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. An adjective answers what kind, which one, or how many about a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Those other questions belong to adverbs. An adjective answers what kind, which one, and how many.

questions.text:
In this sentence, which word does the adjective "strong" describe?

"It is flanked with strong towers."

answers.text: towers
flanked
it
with

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Strong tells what kind of towers, so it describes the noun towers.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An adjective describes a noun. Find the noun that strong is telling you about.

questions.text: The words a, an, and the are a special kind of adjective. What are they called?

answers.text: prepositions
article adjectives
subject pronouns
linking verbs

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A, an, and the are article adjectives. They point to a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A, an, and the always point to a noun. They are called article adjectives.

questions.text:
An adverb describes a verb. Which word is the adverb in this sentence?

"Gulliver passed gently through the streets."

answers.text: Gulliver
passed
gently
streets

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gently tells how Gulliver passed, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb passed, then ask "passed how?" The answer is the adverb.

questions.text: Which set of questions does an adverb answer?

answers.text: How? When? Where? To what extent?
What kind? Which one? How many?
Who or what?
Whose is it?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. An adverb answers how, when, where, or to what extent.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "What kind, which one, how many" belong to adjectives. An adverb answers how, when, where, or to what extent.

questions.text: In "The horses were daily led before me," what question does "daily" answer?

answers.text: How?
Where?
To what extent?
When?

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Daily tells when the horses were led, so it answers "when."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Daily tells you how often something happened, which is a "when" question.

questions.text:
Not every adverb ends in -ly. Which word is the adverb in this sentence?

"His chains were immediately unlocked."

answers.text: chains
were
immediately
unlocked

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Immediately tells when the chains were unlocked, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "unlocked when?" The word that answers is the adverb.

questions.text: In Chapter 3, how does someone win a high government office in Lilliput?

answers.text: By winning a written exam.
By being born into a noble family.
By jumping the highest on a rope without falling.
By the longest service in the army.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Candidates dance on a rope, and whoever jumps highest without falling gets the office.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the part about the rope-dancers in Chapter 3.

questions.text: An inference is best described as:

answers.text: A fact the text states directly.
A smart conclusion you build from a detail plus what you know.
A summary of the whole chapter.
A wild guess with no support.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. An inference is supported by a detail you can point to, but the text does not state it outright.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An inference is not stated on the page and is not a wild guess. It is a conclusion you build from evidence.

questions.text: In Chapter 4, what is the war between Lilliput and Blefuscu actually about?

answers.text: Gold and territory.
A stolen crown.
The right to fish the channel.
Which end of an egg people should crack.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The two empires went to war over whether to break an egg at the big end or the small end.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Reldresal's explanation in Chapter 4. The cause is smaller than it sounds.

questions.text: The story of Gulliver's Travels is told in first-person point of view. What does that mean for the reader?

answers.text: We see the events through Gulliver's eyes only, and he chooses what to tell.
A narrator outside the story sees everyone's thoughts.
The reader is a character in the story.
The story has no narrator at all.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Gulliver uses "I" and can only show us what he saw and chose to share.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First person means one character, Gulliver, narrates with "I" and controls what we see.

questions.text: In Chapter 5, why does the emperor begin to turn against Gulliver?

answers.text: Gulliver loses a battle.
Gulliver refuses to help enslave all of Blefuscu.
Gulliver steals from the treasury.
Gulliver tries to leave the country.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gulliver will not help bring "a free and brave people into slavery," and the emperor never forgives him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the moment after Gulliver brings back the fleet, when the emperor wants more.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is an ADJECTIVE? "The rope-dancers performed upon a slender thread."

answers.text: performed
thread
slender
upon

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Slender tells what kind of thread, so it is an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what kind of thread?" The describing word is the adjective.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is an ADVERB? "Gulliver passed gently through the streets."

answers.text: Gulliver
streets
through
gently

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gently tells how Gulliver passed, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb passed, then ask "passed how?" The answer is the adverb.

questions.text: In Chapter 6, Swift describes Lilliput's laws as fairly wise, but the court itself runs on rope-dancing and a jealous treasurer's lies. What is Swift doing with that gap?

answers.text: Showing that the laws are useless.
Quietly mocking how far a real government can fall from its own good ideals.
Explaining how to write good laws.
Praising the emperor's wisdom.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The gap between the wise laws and the foolish court is Swift's point about real governments.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Notice the difference between the laws Swift praises and the court behavior he shows. The gap is the point.

questions.text: A conjunction is a word that does what?

answers.text: Names a person, place, or thing.
Joins words, groups of words, or ideas.
Describes a noun.
Shows an action.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A conjunction is a joining word. It links two things together.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A conjunction sits between two things and connects them. Look for the option about joining.

questions.text:
Which word is the conjunction in this sentence?

"Gulliver mended the boat and gathered his oars."

answers.text: mended
boat
and
oars

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. And joins the two action verbs, mended and gathered, so it is a conjunction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the little word that links the two actions. That is the conjunction.

questions.text:
Which word is the conjunction in this sentence?

"The court would take his eyes or his life."

answers.text: court
take
eyes
or

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Or joins the two choices, his eyes or his life, so it is a conjunction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which word offers a choice between two things? That is the conjunction.

questions.text: In "He fled to Blefuscu, but the court still hunted him," what job does the conjunction "but" do?

answers.text: It shows a turn or contrast.
It adds one action to another.
It offers a choice.
It names a place.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. But marks a turn: he escaped, and yet the court kept after him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: But signals a turn or surprise. It does not add or offer a choice.

questions.text: A pronoun is a word that does what?

answers.text: Joins two ideas together.
Tells how many.
Takes the place of a noun.
Shows an action.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A pronoun stands in for a noun so you do not repeat the same name. Words like he, she, it, and they are pronouns.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A pronoun replaces a noun. Words like he, she, it, and they are pronouns.

questions.text:
Which word is the subject pronoun in this sentence?

"The lord came at night, and he warned Gulliver."

answers.text: lord
he
night
warned

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He stands in for the lord and is the subject of "warned," so it is a subject pronoun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the short word that stands in for the lord and does the warning. That is the subject pronoun.

questions.text: In "Gulliver fixed the boat and rowed it away," which noun does the pronoun "it" stand for?

answers.text: Gulliver
away
the boat
rowed

questions.feedback_correct: Right. It stands for the boat, the thing Gulliver fixed and rowed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask what "it" stands for. The pronoun points back to the boat.

questions.text: In Chapter 7, what is the title of the document drawn up against Gulliver?

answers.text: A royal pardon.
Articles of impeachment charging him with treason.
A trade agreement with Blefuscu.
A list of his rewards.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The articles of impeachment charge Gulliver, called Quinbus Flestrin, with treason.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the secret warning in Chapter 7. The lord shows Gulliver a list of charges.

questions.text: The Lilliputian court calls one proposed punishment an act of great mercy. What is it?

answers.text: Sending him home with gifts.
Letting him keep his title.
Putting out his eyes instead of executing him.
A small fine.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The council treats blinding Gulliver, rather than killing him, as great mercy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the council's debate. The "merciful" sentence is still harsh.

questions.text: A narrator is best described as:

answers.text: The author's home country.
The voice that tells the story.
The main problem in a plot.
A describing word.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The narrator is the voice telling the story. In this book, that voice is Gulliver.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The narrator is who tells the story. Here it is Gulliver, speaking as "I."

questions.text: Why should a reader be careful trusting everything Gulliver says about his trial?

answers.text: Because he is lying about every event.
Because he was not actually there.
Because he is the only narrator and is the person on trial, so he may shape the telling.
Because the trial never happened.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Gulliver mostly reports honestly, but he is on trial, so a careful reader weighs how he shapes the story.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The point is not that he lies. It is that one narrator, who is on trial, controls what we see.

questions.text: In Chapter 8, how does Gulliver finally get home?

answers.text: The emperor of Lilliput forgives him.
He flees to Blefuscu, repairs an overturned boat, and sails away.
He is carried home by an eagle.
He stays in Lilliput for the rest of his life.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He escapes to Blefuscu, finds and repairs a boat, and is picked up by an English ship.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the end of Chapter 8. Gulliver finds a way off the islands by sea.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a CONJUNCTION? "Gulliver mended the boat and gathered his oars."

answers.text: mended
and
boat
oars

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. And joins the two actions, mended and gathered, so it is a conjunction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the word that links the two actions. That joining word is the conjunction.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a PRONOUN? "The lord came at night, and he warned Gulliver."

answers.text: lord
night
he
warned

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He stands in for the lord, so it is a pronoun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the word that stands in for the lord. That word is the pronoun.

questions.text: A good summary of Part I would do which of these?

answers.text: Include every small detail in order.
Keep the main events and leave out small details and personal opinions.
Tell only the writer's opinion of the story.
Copy the chapter word for word.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A summary keeps the events the story turns on and drops the small details and opinions.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A summary is short and fair. It keeps the main events, not every detail or your opinion.

questions.text: An interjection is best described as:

answers.text: the word that tells what is being said about the subject
a word or short phrase that bursts out to show feeling
a word that connects two complete sentences
the specific name of a person or place

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. An interjection shows sudden feeling and is not tied to the rest of the sentence by grammar.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about words like Oh, Wow, and Alas. They show feeling and can be lifted out of the sentence.

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence is the interjection?

"Yikes, the cat looked three times larger than an ox!"

answers.text: cat
larger
Yikes
looked

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Yikes bursts out to show fear, and you could remove it and still have a full sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the short feeling-word at the front, set off by a comma.

questions.text: In the sentence "The HUGE creature waded after the boat," what part of speech is the word in capitals?

answers.text: verb
adjective
subject noun
adverb

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Huge answers "what kind of creature?" so it is an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "which one? what kind? how many?" A word that answers those about a noun is an adjective.

questions.text: In the sentence "The reapers QUICKLY moved through the field," what part of speech is the word in capitals?

answers.text: adverb
adjective
subject noun
preposition

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Quickly answers "moved how?" so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "how? when? where? to what extent?" A word that answers those about a verb is an adverb.

questions.text: In the sentence "The farmer placed Gulliver UPON a table," what part of speech is the word in capitals?

answers.text: conjunction
subject noun
adverb
preposition

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Upon shows a relationship and starts a phrase, so it is a preposition. Table is the object of the preposition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which word shows a relationship of place and starts a phrase that ends in a noun? That is a preposition.

questions.text: In the sentence "Glumdalclitch loved Gulliver, and SHE protected him," what part of speech is the word in capitals?

answers.text: subject noun
verb
subject pronoun
adjective

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. She is the doer and it replaces the noun Glumdalclitch, so it is a subject pronoun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "who or what protected?" The doer is a pronoun standing in for a noun, so it is a subject pronoun.

questions.text: In the sentence "ALAS, the storm drove the ship far off course," what part of speech is the word in capitals?

answers.text: interjection
subject noun
preposition
conjunction

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Alas bursts out to show feeling and can be lifted out, so it is an interjection.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Which word shows feeling and could be removed without breaking the sentence? That is an interjection.

questions.text: In the sentence "Gulliver feared the giant CAT at the dinner table," what part of speech is the word in capitals?

answers.text: verb
adverb
subject noun
noun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Cat names a thing here, so it is a noun. (It is not the doer, so it is not the subject noun.)
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "who or what?" A word that names a person, place, thing, or idea is a noun. The doer of the sentence is Gulliver, so cat is not the subject noun.

questions.text: In Part II, how is Gulliver's situation different from Part I?

answers.text: He is now a giant among tiny people.
He is now a tiny man among giants.
He is the same size as everyone around him.
He never leaves England.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The scale flips. In Brobdingnag, Gulliver is the small one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember the perspective flip: in Lilliput he was huge, but in Brobdingnag he is tiny.

questions.text: How does Gulliver first end up among the giants?

answers.text: The emperor of Brobdingnag invites him.
He is born in Brobdingnag.
A storm blows his ship off course and he is left behind on shore.
He builds a boat and sails there on purpose.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A storm carries the ship off course, and Gulliver is stranded when the crew rows away.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the start of Part II, Chapter 1, after the storm.

questions.text: Gulliver says that "nothing is great or little otherwise than by comparison." This means:

answers.text: size and importance depend on what you stand beside.
giants are always more important than small people.
only kings and queens truly matter.
comparison is a waste of time.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A thing is only big or small next to something else. Gulliver is the same man in both lands.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how Gulliver felt mighty in Lilliput but helpless in Brobdingnag, though he never changed size.

questions.text: When the king of Brobdingnag hears Gulliver brag about Europe, he concludes that human grandeur is:

answers.text: the greatest thing he has ever heard of.
contemptible, since a tiny creature can mimic it completely.
too complicated for him to understand.
a secret he must keep from his court.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. If a six-inch creature can copy human pride so well, the king reasons, that pride is not as grand as humans think.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the king's speech in Chapter 3 about "diminutive insects."

questions.text: Which of these is the best example of imagery (a vivid word picture for the senses)?

answers.text: The kingdom contained fifty-one cities.
Gulliver was bought by the queen.
Glumdalclitch was the farmer's daughter.
The queen would "craunch the wing of a lark, bones and all, between her teeth."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. You can almost hear and see the crunch. That is imagery.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Imagery makes a picture for your senses. Look for the line you can hear or see most clearly.

questions.text: A strong reader supports a claim about the text by:

answers.text: quoting an exact line and adding a citation.
guessing what probably happened.
repeating the claim louder.
summarizing the whole book.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Claim plus quoted evidence plus a citation is the move you practiced on Friday.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember the three-step move: claim, then quoted evidence, then a chapter citation.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is an INTERJECTION? "Yikes, the giant cat turned toward me!"

answers.text: cat
turned
toward
Yikes

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Yikes bursts out to show feeling and can be lifted out of the sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the short feeling-word that could be removed and still leave a complete sentence.

questions.text: What is the part of speech of the word in capitals? "The huge farmer GENTLY lifted Gulliver."

answers.text: adverb
adjective
noun
conjunction

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gently tells how the farmer lifted Gulliver, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "lifted how?" A word that answers a how question is an adverb.

questions.text: A complete sentence is built from two main parts. What are they?

answers.text: A noun and an adjective.
The subject and the predicate.
A question and an answer.
A preposition and its object.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject tells who or what, and the predicate tells what is being said about the subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Every complete sentence is built from a subject and a predicate.

questions.text:
What is the SUBJECT in this sentence?

"The king was struck with horror at the description."

answers.text: horror
description
king
struck

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Find the verb "was struck," then ask "Who or what was struck?" The king was, so "king" is the subject noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb "was struck," then ask "Who or what was struck?" The answer is the subject noun.

questions.text:
What is the SUBJECT in this sentence, and is it a subject noun or a subject pronoun?

"In this manner I had several conversations with him."

answers.text: I, a subject pronoun
manner, a subject noun
conversations, a subject noun
him, a subject pronoun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject is not always the first words. Ask "Who or what had conversations?" The answer is "I," a subject pronoun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The subject is not the opening phrase. Find the verb "had," then ask "Who or what had conversations?" The answer "I" is a subject pronoun.

questions.text: Which group of words is a complete sentence (it has both a subject and a predicate)?

answers.text: The tiny comb made of beard stumps.
Running sideways along the bench.
After the long concert at court.
Gulliver played a jig.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Gulliver" is the subject and "played a jig" is the predicate, so it is a complete sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complete sentence needs a subject and a predicate. Which choice names who AND tells what is being said about them?

questions.text: A phrase is a group of words that:

answers.text: always has its own subject and verb.
is always a complete sentence.
work together but do not have their own subject and verb.
must end with a verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A phrase works as one unit but is not a complete sentence on its own.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A phrase has no subject and verb of its own. That is what makes it a phrase, not a complete sentence.

questions.text:
Which group of words is a prepositional phrase?

"I now perceived I was fallen into the sea."

answers.text: I perceived
into the sea
was fallen
now perceived

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "into the sea" begins with the preposition "into" and ends with "sea," the object of the preposition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for a preposition like "into" that opens the group, then the noun that ends it. That noun is the object of the preposition.

questions.text:
In the phrase "with great attention," which word is the OBJECT OF THE PREPOSITION?

"The king heard me with great attention."

answers.text: king
heard
great
attention

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "with" is the preposition, and "attention" is the noun it points to, so "attention" is the object of the preposition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The object of the preposition is the noun after the preposition. After "with" comes "attention."

questions.text: In Chapter 6, why does Gulliver give the king a long, glowing account of England?

answers.text: He wants the king to admire England and Gulliver himself.
The king forces him to confess England's crimes.
He is trying to start a war with Brobdingnag.
He has been ordered to write a history book.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gulliver is proud of England and hopes the king will be impressed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the start of the conversation. Gulliver is praising his country out of pride.

questions.text: What does the king of Brobdingnag finally conclude about Gulliver's countrymen?

answers.text: They are the wisest people he has heard of.
They are gentle and harmless.
They are "the most pernicious race of little odious vermin."
They should rule all of Brobdingnag.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The king's harsh verdict grows out of Gulliver's own proud account.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The king's judgment is harsh. Reread his speech at the end of Chapter 6.

questions.text: A THEME is best described as:

answers.text: the order of events in a story.
a big idea about life that an author builds across a story.
a list of the characters.
the place where a story happens.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The theme of this part of the book is human pride.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A theme is not the plot or the setting. It is the big idea, here, pride.

questions.text: In Chapter 7, why does the king refuse Gulliver's offer of gunpowder?

answers.text: He already has a better weapon.
He thinks the recipe is fake.
He cannot afford to make it.
He is horrified by such cruelty and would rather lose half his kingdom.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The king is struck with horror and forbids Gulliver to mention it again.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the king's reaction. He is horrified, not unable, to use it.

questions.text: In Chapter 7, the king says the person who does the MOST good for a country is the one who:

answers.text: wins the most battles.
writes the most laws.
makes two ears of corn grow where one grew before.
collects the most taxes.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He values the corn-grower over "the whole race of politicians put together."
questions.feedback_incorrect: The king praises useful work, not war or politics. Reread his opinion about the corn.

questions.text: In Chapter 8, how does Gulliver finally escape Brobdingnag?

answers.text: He builds a tiny boat and sails away.
An eagle carries off his box and drops it into the sea, where a ship finds him.
The king sets him free as a reward.
He digs a tunnel under the palace.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. An eagle seizes his travelling-box, drops it in the sea, and an English ship rescues him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the escape. A giant bird is the reason Gulliver ends up in the ocean.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is the SUBJECT? "The carpenter sawed a passage in the cover."

answers.text: passage
carpenter
cover
sawed

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "who sawed?" The carpenter did, so the carpenter is the subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb "sawed," then ask who did it. The answer is the subject.

questions.text: Which group of words is a PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE? "I now perceived I was fallen into the sea."

answers.text: I perceived
was fallen
into the sea
now

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "into the sea" begins with the preposition into and ends with the noun sea.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the small place word that opens a group ending in a noun.

questions.text: What does every clause have?

answers.text: Only a verb.
Its own subject and its own verb.
A preposition and an object of the preposition.
At least two sentences.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A clause is a group of words with its own subject and its own verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A clause always has both a subject and a verb. That is what makes it a clause.

questions.text: Which group of words is an INDEPENDENT clause (it can stand alone as a sentence)?

answers.text: When I was a little refreshed.
The two horses came up close to me.
Because the road was beaten.
Although the horse looked mild.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The subject noun is "horses" and the verb is "came," and the clause can stand alone, so it is independent.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the choice that could be a complete sentence by itself, with no opening word that makes it lean.

questions.text: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause (it cannot stand alone)?

answers.text: I wrote the words down.
The mare rose from her mat.
Because they looked upon it as a prodigy.
Gulliver drank the milk.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The word "because" makes the clause lean on the rest of the sentence, so it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dependent clause begins with a word like because, when, or although that leaves you waiting for more.

questions.text: What is the difference between a dependent clause and a phrase?

answers.text: A dependent clause has a subject and a verb; a phrase does not.
A phrase is always longer.
There is no difference.
A phrase can stand alone; a clause cannot.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Both can be part of a sentence, but only a clause has its own subject and verb. "In the country" is a phrase; "When I was refreshed" is a clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "In the country" is a phrase, with no subject and no verb. "When I was refreshed" is a clause, with a subject and a verb.

questions.text: A SIMPLE sentence is made of:

answers.text: two dependent clauses.
three or more clauses.
one dependent clause only.
one independent clause.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A simple sentence is one independent clause that stands alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A simple sentence has just one clause that can stand alone by itself.

questions.text: What type is this sentence? "I drew my hanger, and I gave him a good blow."

answers.text: Compound
Simple
Complex
It is not a sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both clauses can stand alone, joined by the conjunction "and," so it is compound.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each side of "and" could be its own sentence, so two independent clauses joined makes it compound.

questions.text: What type is this sentence? "When the beast felt the smart, he drew back."

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
A phrase

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The dependent clause "When the beast felt the smart" leans on the independent clause, so it is complex.
questions.feedback_incorrect: One clause begins with "when" and cannot stand alone. An independent clause plus a dependent clause makes a complex sentence.

questions.text: Read this sentence: "When I offered to slacken my pace, he would cry hhuun hhuun." Which part is the DEPENDENT clause?

answers.text: he would cry hhuun hhuun
When I offered to slacken my pace
he would cry
hhuun hhuun

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It begins with "when," so it leans on the independent clause and cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the clause that begins with "when." That opening word makes it dependent.

questions.text: How does Gulliver end up alone on the shore of this strange country?

answers.text: A storm wrecks his ship.
His own crew turns pirate and sets him ashore.
The Houyhnhnms capture him.
He chooses to stay behind.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. His crew, full of buccaneers he recruited, mutinies and leaves him on the coast.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Chapter 1. Gulliver's own men conspire against him and put him ashore.

questions.text: What are the Houyhnhnms?

answers.text: Tiny people, like the Lilliputians.
Giant humans, like the Brobdingnagians.
Calm, reasoning horses who rule the country.
A kind of monkey.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Houyhnhnms are horses governed by reason, and their name means "the perfection of nature."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Chapters 1 and 3. The wise rulers of this land are horses.

questions.text: Why is Gulliver so disturbed to learn what the Yahoos are?

answers.text: The Yahoos can speak his language.
The Yahoos are larger than him.
The Yahoos own all the shining stones.
The Yahoos look exactly like humans, including Gulliver.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. To his "everlasting mortification," Gulliver sees the Yahoo has "a perfect human figure" like his own.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Chapter 2. The horror is that the filthy Yahoos are shaped just like people.

questions.text: The Houyhnhnms have no word in their language for which idea?

answers.text: Lying or falsehood.
Grass or oats.
Day or night.
Cold or heat.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Because they always tell the truth, they have no word for lying. The master can barely grasp the idea.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Chapters 3 and 4. There is one human habit they cannot even name.

questions.text: In Chapter 5, what does the master horse decide a soldier is?

answers.text: The bravest kind of human.
A Yahoo hired to kill others of his own kind.
A protector of the weak.
A wise leader of nations.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He calls a soldier "a Yahoo hired to kill, in cold blood, as many of his own species" as he can.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the master's view of war in Chapter 5. He sees no honor in it.

questions.text: What is the THEME of Part IV, the big idea Swift builds about human nature?

answers.text: Horses make better pets than dogs.
Travel is always dangerous.
Humans use their reason to feed their worst appetites rather than to govern them.
England is the greatest country on earth.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The master decides humans have "some small pittance of reason" used to "aggravate our natural corruptions."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A theme is a claim about life. Swift's claim is about how humans misuse reason.

questions.text: Which sentence is a COMPLEX sentence (one independent and one dependent clause)?

answers.text: The two horses came up close to me.
When the beast felt the smart, he drew back.
I drew my hanger, and I gave him a good blow.
The mare rose from her mat.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "When the beast felt the smart" is a dependent clause leaning on the independent clause, so it is complex.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the sentence with a clause that begins with a word like "when" and cannot stand alone.

questions.text: Which group of words is a DEPENDENT clause (it cannot stand alone)?

answers.text: Gulliver drank the milk.
The carpenter came.
The horses confer together.
Because they looked upon him as a prodigy.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The word "because" makes the clause lean on the rest of the sentence, so it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dependent clause begins with a word like because, when, or although and leaves you waiting for more.

questions.text: A clause is a group of words that always contains:

answers.text: a subject and a verb
an exclamation point
at least one article adjective
a question word

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Every clause has a subject and a verb. A complete sentence is built from at least one independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The two parts every clause must have are a subject and a verb.

questions.text: What is the purpose of this sentence? "Take care of thyself, gentle Yahoo."

answers.text: It asks a question (interrogative).
It makes a statement (declarative).
It gives a request or command (imperative).
It shows strong feeling (exclamatory).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It tells someone to do something, with an understood subject "you," so it is imperative.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask who is being told to do something. The subject "you" is understood, so it is imperative.

questions.text: What is the purpose of this sentence? "Whether the Yahoos should be exterminated from the face of the earth?"

answers.text: interrogative (asks)
declarative (tells)
imperative (commands)
exclamatory (exclaims)

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The question mark and the asking job make it interrogative.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the end mark. A question mark signals an interrogative sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence is exclamatory (shows strong feeling and ends with an exclamation point)?

answers.text: "I finished a sort of Indian canoe."
"They calculate the year by the revolution of the sun and moon."
"He milked their cows and reaped their oats."
"...this execrable crew of butchers... is a modern colony!"

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The strong feeling and the exclamation point make it exclamatory.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An exclamatory sentence ends in "!" and carries strong feeling. Find the one that does.

questions.text: In "I had worked two chairs with my knife," what part of speech is "knife"?

answers.text: verb
adjective
noun
adverb

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Knife" names a thing, so it is a noun. It is also the object of the preposition "with."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "worked with what?" The answer names a thing, so it is a noun.

questions.text: In "I had worked two chairs with my knife," what part of speech is "two"?

answers.text: noun
adjective
verb
conjunction

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Two" answers "How many chairs?" so it describes the noun and is an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "How many chairs?" A word that describes a noun is an adjective.

questions.text: In "I fell into a swoon at his feet," what part of speech is "into"?

answers.text: conjunction
adverb
preposition
noun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Into" begins a phrase ending in a noun ("a swoon"), so it is a preposition. "Swoon" is its object of the preposition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: It begins a group of words ending in a noun ("a swoon"). That is a preposition.

questions.text: In Chapter 9, what does the grand assembly of the Houyhnhnms debate?

answers.text: whether to make Gulliver their king
whether the Yahoos should be exterminated
whether to go to war with Brobdingnag
whether to learn to read and write

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The only debate in their country is whether the Yahoos should be wiped out.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the start of Chapter 9. The assembly debates the fate of the Yahoos.

questions.text: FORESHADOWING is best described as:

answers.text: a summary at the end of a story
the place where a story happens
a clue planted early that hints at something later
a long description of a character

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Foreshadowing is an early clue that points to something that happens later.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Foreshadowing reaches forward. It is an early clue about what is coming.

questions.text: In Chapter 10, why must Gulliver leave the country of the Houyhnhnms?

answers.text: The assembly decides it is not natural for a horse to keep a Yahoo like him.
He commits a crime and is punished.
He grows homesick and asks to go.
The Yahoos drive him out by force.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The assembly exhorts his master to send him away, and his master cannot refuse.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the master's news in Chapter 10. The assembly objects to a horse keeping a Yahoo as a companion.

questions.text: A DYNAMIC character is one who:

answers.text: stays exactly the same all through the story
appears in only one scene
never speaks
changes in an important way across the story

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Gulliver is dynamic. The man who comes home is not the man who left.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dynamic character changes. A character who stays the same is static.

questions.text: Which detail best shows how much Gulliver has changed by the end of Chapter 11?

answers.text: He builds a canoe out of Yahoo skins.
He learns the Houyhnhnm language.
He faints when his own wife hugs him, and prefers his horses to his family.
He sails toward New Holland.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Fainting at his wife's touch and choosing horses over people shows a deep change.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the detail that shows his feelings about people have flipped, not just an event.

questions.text: In Chapter 12, what is the one human vice Gulliver says he cannot tolerate above all others?

answers.text: laziness
pride
curiosity
forgetfulness

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A "lump of deformity... smitten with pride" is what breaks his patience. Pride is Swift's main target.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the end of Chapter 12. The vice that breaks Gulliver's patience is pride.

questions.text: What is the PURPOSE of this sentence? "Take care of thyself, gentle Yahoo."

answers.text: interrogative (it asks)
exclamatory (it exclaims)
declarative (it tells)
imperative (it gives a request or command)

questions.feedback_correct: Right. It tells someone to do something, with an understood "you," so it is imperative.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask who is being told to do something. A request or command is imperative.

questions.text: In "I had worked two chairs with my knife," what part of speech is the word "with"?

answers.text: preposition
verb
adjective
conjunction

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "With" shows a relationship and begins a phrase ending in a noun, so it is a preposition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The word begins a group ending in a noun ("my knife"). That is a preposition.

quizzes.title: Module 1 Outro — Looking Back
quizzes.description: You have finished the reading and the project work for Module 1. Take a few minutes to look back. Answer honestly. This is how your teacher learns what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. Look back at how you answered this in the Module Intro: **How does changing your perspective change what you see, in others and in yourself?

Answer it again now, in three or four sentences, using something specific from Gulliver's voyages. How has your answer changed since the start?

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)
Confidence rating. How confident do you feel that you can explain what Swift says about human pride and use details from the book to back it up?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about Gulliver's Travels, the theme of pride, or the writing skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. This module is about pride and seeing yourself clearly. Pick the ONE virtue Gulliver most needed, and that this module asked of you:

answers.text: Honesty (telling the truth, even about yourself)
Self-government (controlling your own pride and judging yourself fairly)
Perseverance (sticking with hard reading and finishing the project)
Another of the seven virtues

questions.text: Explain your choice above in two or three sentences.

quizzes.title: Module 2 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description: Welcome to Module 2. You will read The Call of the Wild by Jack London, the story of a dog named Buck who is stolen from a comfortable home and forced to survive in the frozen North. By the end he is a changed creature. Before you begin, answer a few quick questions. There are no wrong answers here. Your first thoughts give your teacher a starting point.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **What transforms Buck from a pampered house dog into a creature of the wild, and what does his change reveal about instinct, survival, and the pull between civilization and the wild?

In two or three sentences, give your first answer. You have not read the book yet, so just say what you expect: what do you think changes a creature the most, and is changing always a bad thing? You will come back to this question many times.

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. By the end of this module you will be able to:

- [ ] Read and follow Buck's journey across all seven chapters, from Judge Miller's place to the call of the wild. - [ ] Explain how London uses setting, instinct, and survival to show a character changing. - [ ] Notice and name craft moves such as tone, figurative language, and symbol, and find them in the text. - [ ] Build one argument step by step: a thesis, evidence with explanation, a counterclaim, and a conclusion. - [ ] Build one Reading Journal all module long and use it to grow your project argument. - [ ] Write an argumentative essay and create a visual and a VR scene that show Buck's transformation.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
One thing you are curious about. Name one thing about survival in the wild, about animals and instinct, or about this book that you are curious to find out. One sentence is fine.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal.)

A direct object receives the action of the verb. Which word is the direct object in this sentence?

"Manuel doubled a rope around Buck's neck."

answers.text: Manuel
doubled
rope
neck

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "Manuel doubled what?" The answer is rope, so rope is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the action verb, then ask "Manuel doubled what?" The answer is the direct object.

questions.text: Which question finds the direct object?

answers.text: Subject verb to whom or for whom?
Subject verb what or whom?
What kind, which one, how many?
How, when, where, to what extent?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After the action verb, ask "what or whom?" to find the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The direct object answers "what or whom?" right after the action verb. "To whom or for whom" finds the indirect object.

questions.text:
Which word is the direct object in this sentence?

"He drank the water eagerly."

answers.text: eagerly
He
drank
water

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "He drank what?" The answer is water, so water is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the action verb drank, then ask "drank what?" The answer is the direct object.

questions.text:
An indirect object names the one the action is done to or for. Which word is the indirect object in this sentence?

"The man brought Buck water."

answers.text: Buck
water
man
brought

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The water was brought to Buck, so Buck is the indirect object. Water is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First find the direct object (water), then ask "brought water to whom?" The answer is the indirect object.

questions.text: Which question finds the indirect object?

answers.text: Who or what verb?
What kind or which one?
Verb plus direct object, to whom or for whom?
How or when?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After you find the direct object, ask "to whom or for whom?" to find the indirect object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The indirect object answers "to whom or for whom?" once you already have the direct object.

questions.text:
In this sentence, which word is the INDIRECT object?

"Perrault paid the man three hundred dollars."

answers.text: Perrault
man
dollars
paid

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The dollars were paid to the man, so man is the indirect object. Dollars is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dollars is the direct object (paid what?). The man is who it was paid to, so the man is the indirect object.

questions.text:
In this sentence, which word is the DIRECT object?

"The North taught Buck a hard lesson."

answers.text: Buck
North
taught
lesson

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "taught what?" The answer is lesson, so lesson is the direct object. Buck is the indirect object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Buck is who the lesson was taught to (indirect object). The thing taught, the lesson, is the direct object.

questions.text: Which is true about indirect objects?

answers.text: A sentence can have an indirect object with no direct object.
The indirect object answers "how" or "when."
The indirect object always comes after the direct object.
You cannot have an indirect object without a direct object.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The indirect object names who the direct object is given to or done for, so there must be a direct object first.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The indirect object names who receives the direct object, so a direct object must be present. It also sits before the direct object, not after.

questions.text: Where does Buck live at the start of Chapter 1?

answers.text: On a fishing boat off Seattle.
In a kennel in the Klondike.
At Judge Miller's place in the Santa Clara Valley.
In a city apartment in San Francisco.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck rules Judge Miller's estate in the warm, sun-kissed Santa Clara Valley.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening pages. Buck's home is a large California estate.

questions.text: What kind of dog is Buck before he is taken away?

answers.text: A small, spoiled lapdog who never goes outside.
A strong, proud dog who rules the estate and keeps his body hard with outdoor life.
A wild dog that has never lived with people.
A sled dog already trained for the snow.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. London shows Buck as king of the estate, proud, and kept hard by hunting and swimming, not soft.
questions.feedback_incorrect: London is careful to say Buck is not a pampered house-dog. Hunting kept his muscles hard.

questions.text: How does Buck end up leaving the estate?

answers.text: The Judge sells him to a dog-doctor.
He runs away on his own.
He is lost during a hunt.
Manuel, a gardener's helper, secretly sells him for gambling money.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Manuel betrays Buck and sells him to a stranger to pay his gambling debts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the night of Manuel's treachery. A gardener's helper leads Buck away and sells him.

questions.text: London writes that Buck was "metamorphosed into a raging fiend" during the express-car ride. What does this show?

answers.text: The harsh treatment is already changing the kind of creature Buck is.
Buck has caught a disease.
Buck has decided to obey everyone.
Buck is only pretending to be angry.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The new, brutal setting is transforming the comfortable Buck into something fierce.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Metamorphosed" means changed completely. The cruelty and hunger are remaking Buck.

questions.text: What lesson does the man in the red sweater teach Buck with the club?

answers.text: That Buck should always fight harder.
That a man with a club is a master to be obeyed.
That men can never be trusted at all.
That Buck is free to leave.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London calls it Buck's introduction to "the reign of primitive law": the club beats raw fury, so a man with one is a master.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the beating. London says the club is "a revelation" about who holds power in this new world.

questions.text: In the sentence "Buck had accepted the rope," which word is the DIRECT object?

answers.text: Buck
accepted
rope
had

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "Buck accepted what?" The answer is rope, so rope is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the action verb, then ask "accepted what?" The answer is the direct object.

questions.text: In the sentence "The man brought Buck water," which word is the INDIRECT object?

answers.text: man
water
brought
Buck

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The water was brought to Buck, so Buck is the indirect object. Water is the direct object.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First find the direct object (water), then ask "brought water to whom?" The answer is Buck.

questions.text: A "dynamic character" is one who:

answers.text: appears in many scenes.
changes over the course of the story.
never speaks.
is always the hero.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Buck is a dynamic character. The events of the story change who he is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dynamic character changes through the story. Buck is the clearest example.

questions.text: A transitive verb passes its action to a receiver. What question finds that receiver?

answers.text: How? When? Where?
The verb plus "whom?" or "what?"
Who or what does the action?
Whose is it?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After the action verb, ask "whom?" or "what?" If the sentence answers, the verb is transitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To find a receiver, ask the verb "whom?" or "what?" The "how, when, where" questions belong to adverbs.

questions.text:
Is the verb transitive or intransitive?

"Pike slyly stole a slice of bacon."

answers.text: Transitive, because "stole what? a slice of bacon."
Intransitive, because there is no receiver.
Transitive, because "slyly" is the receiver.
Intransitive, because "stole" cannot take an object.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Stole what? A slice of bacon. The action lands on a receiver, so stole is transitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "stole what?" The sentence answers: a slice of bacon. That receiver makes the verb transitive.

questions.text:
Is the verb transitive or intransitive?

"Buck toiled in the traces."

answers.text: Transitive, because "the traces" is the receiver.
Intransitive, because "toiled whom or what?" has no answer.
Transitive, because "in" points to a receiver.
Intransitive, because "toiled" is a linking verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Toiled whom or what? Nothing answers. "In the traces" tells where, not what, so toiled is intransitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "toiled whom or what?" There is no receiver. "In the traces" tells where. So the verb is intransitive.

questions.text: In which sentence is the bold verb intransitive (no receiver)?

answers.text: "He bit the ice from his toes."
"Buck hauled the sled."
"On the cold nights Buck howled long and wolflike."
"Pike stole the bacon."
