questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Howled whom or what? Nothing answers. "Long and wolflike" tells how, so howled is intransitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Test each verb with "whom or what?" Howled has no receiver. The others all do.

questions.text: A comma separates items in a series of three or more. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: "Buck learned to haul, to obey and, to steal."
"Buck learned to haul to obey and to steal."
"Buck learned to haul, to obey, and to steal."
"Buck, learned to haul, to obey, and to steal."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Three items in a series each get a comma, including before the "and."
questions.feedback_incorrect: In a series of three, put a comma after each item before the final "and": haul, to obey, and to steal.

questions.text: Use a comma after an introductory word or phrase. Which sentence is correct?

answers.text: "By evening Perrault, secured another dog."
"By evening, Perrault secured another dog."
"By, evening Perrault secured another dog."
"By evening Perrault secured, another dog."

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The introductory phrase "By evening" is followed by a comma before the main sentence begins.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma goes right after the introductory phrase "By evening," not inside the main sentence.

questions.text: In "Spitz, the lead dog, ran out his tongue and laughed," why are there commas around "the lead dog"?

answers.text: It begins a new sentence.
It is a series of three items.
It is an interrupter that renames Spitz and could be lifted out.
It is the receiver of the verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "The lead dog" renames Spitz and could be removed without breaking the sentence, so commas set it off on both sides.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "The lead dog" simply renames Spitz. You could lift it out and the sentence still works, so a pair of commas sets it off.

questions.text: Which sentence places ALL its commas correctly?

answers.text: "Cold, hungry, and tired Buck dug a nest in the snow."
"Cold, hungry, and tired, Buck dug a nest in the snow."
"Cold hungry and tired, Buck dug a nest in the snow."
"Cold, hungry and tired, Buck, dug a nest in the snow."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The three describing words form a series, and the whole introductory group is closed off with a comma before "Buck."
questions.feedback_incorrect: You need commas between the three describing words and one more comma after the introductory group, before "Buck."

questions.text: What is "the law of club and fang" in Buck's new world?

answers.text: A set of rules the men teach the dogs in school.
The Southland code of fairness and trust.
The brutal code where the man with the club gives orders and the strongest dog wins.
A treaty between Lilliput and Blefuscu.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The club is the men's power and the fang is the dogs' power. In the Northland there is no other law.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening of Chapter 2. The club belongs to the men, the fang to the dogs, and there is no fair play.

questions.text: What lesson does Buck take from watching the pack kill Curly?

answers.text: Friendly dogs are always safe.
Never go down, because a fallen dog is finished.
The men will always protect the dogs.
Fights are settled fairly, one on one.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Buck sees there is no fair play and once a dog is down, it is over. He vows never to go down.
questions.feedback_incorrect: After Curly falls, the pack closes in and no one saves her. Buck's lesson is to never be the one who goes down.

questions.text: Which is the best example of Buck ADAPTING to survive in Chapter 2?

answers.text: He refuses to pull the sled.
He sleeps in the warm tent every night.
He shares his food with the other dogs.
He learns to eat fast and steal so his ration is not stolen first.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London calls this his adaptability, his capacity to adjust to changing conditions.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Adapting means changing to survive. Buck learns to eat fast and steal, the opposite of his old, fussy habits.

questions.text: Tone is best described as:

answers.text: The order in which events happen.
The attitude or feeling an author builds through word choice.
The number of characters in a chapter.
The setting of the story.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Tone is the feeling the writing gives off, built mostly through the words the author chooses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tone is not the events or setting. It is the attitude an author creates through word choice.

questions.text: London writes that Curly's face "was ripped open from eye to jaw." Which word does the most to build the brutal tone?

answers.text: face
open
ripped
from

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Ripped" is sudden and violent. A milder word like "cut" would soften the whole tone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the most violent word. "Ripped" makes the reader flinch and sets the brutal tone.

questions.text:
Is the verb transitive or intransitive?

"Pike stole a slice of bacon."

answers.text: Intransitive, because there is no receiver.
Transitive, because "stole what? a slice of bacon."
Transitive, because "Pike" is the receiver.
Intransitive, because "slice" tells how.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Stole what? A slice of bacon. The action lands on a receiver, so the verb is transitive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "stole what?" The sentence answers: a slice of bacon. That receiver makes the verb transitive.

questions.text: Which sentence places its commas correctly?

answers.text: "By morning the snow had buried Buck, completely."
"By morning, the snow had buried Buck completely."
"By, morning the snow had buried Buck completely."
"By morning the snow, had buried Buck completely."

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The introductory phrase "By morning" is followed by a comma, and no comma interrupts the main sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma belongs after the introductory phrase "By morning," not inside the main sentence.

questions.text: Which of these works best as a THESIS for an essay about Buck?

answers.text: "Buck is harnessed to a sled in Chapter 2."
"Does Buck change for the better?"
"Buck changes a lot in the Northland."
"Buck gains strength and cunning in the Northland, but he loses the trust and fairness of his old self."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It makes a clear, specific, arguable claim you could defend from the text. That is a thesis.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A thesis takes a specific, arguable side. A fact, a question, or a vague statement will not work as one.

questions.text: A clause that has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a complete sentence is called:

answers.text: a dependent clause
an independent clause
a fragment
a phrase

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. An independent clause is a complete thought and can stand by itself.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The clause that can stand alone as a full sentence is the independent clause.

questions.text:
In this sentence, which part is the dependent clause?

"When Buck finished his ration and returned, he found his nest occupied."

answers.text: he found his nest occupied
When Buck finished his ration and returned
his nest occupied
Buck finished

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The word When makes that part lean on the rest, so it cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The part that starts with When leaves you waiting. That is the dependent clause.

questions.text: A complex sentence is made of:

answers.text: two independent clauses
one independent clause and one dependent clause
two dependent clauses
one phrase and one word

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A complex sentence joins one independent clause with one dependent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence pairs one clause that can stand alone with one that cannot.

questions.text: Which group of words is a sentence FRAGMENT, not a complete sentence?

answers.text: The beast in him roared.
Buck sprang upon Spitz.
Because Spitz had stolen his warm nest.
Spitz was a practised fighter.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It has a subject and verb, but Because makes it depend on more. Standing alone, it is a fragment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the choice that starts with a conjunction and leaves the thought unfinished.

questions.text:
What is the best way to FIX this fragment?

"Because Spitz had stolen his warm nest."

answers.text: Add a comma at the end.
Capitalize the first word.
Join it to a complete thought: "Because Spitz had stolen his warm nest, Buck attacked."
Delete the word Because and leave it as is.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Attaching the dependent clause to an independent clause makes a complete complex sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A fragment needs to be joined to a complete thought, not just repunctuated.

questions.text: A RUN-ON sentence is best described as:

answers.text: a sentence that is too short
two complete thoughts jammed together without correct punctuation or a joining word
a sentence with too many adjectives
a clause that cannot stand alone

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A run-on crowds two complete thoughts together with no period, semicolon, or conjunction to join them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on is two complete thoughts pushed together without correct punctuation or a joining word.

questions.text: Which sentence is a RUN-ON?

answers.text: Buck won the fight, and the team grew calm.
Spitz was beaten Buck became the leader.
After Spitz was beaten, Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten. Buck became the leader.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete thoughts are jammed together with nothing between them. That is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the choice where two full sentences run together with no period, comma and conjunction, or semicolon.

questions.text: Which is a correct way to FIX the run-on "Spitz was beaten Buck became the leader"?

answers.text: Spitz was beaten, Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten Buck, became the leader.
Spitz was beaten. Buck became the leader.
Spitz, was beaten Buck became the leader.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Splitting the run-on into two complete sentences with a period is one correct fix. A semicolon or a comma plus a conjunction would also work.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on is fixed with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word. A comma alone is not enough.

questions.text: What finally makes Buck attack Spitz for the first time, at the camp on Lake Le Barge?

answers.text: Spitz steals Buck's food during a meal.
Spitz takes over Buck's warm sleeping nest.
Spitz attacks François.
Spitz refuses to pull the sled.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. When Buck returns and finds Spitz in his nest, "the beast in him roared," and he springs at Spitz.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the camp scene at Lake Le Barge. The trigger is about Buck's nest.

questions.text: London calls the wild, ancient nature growing in Buck "the dominant primordial beast." What does this mean?

answers.text: Buck is turning into an actual wolf overnight.
The old, wild instincts of Buck's ancestors are taking charge in him.
Buck has caught a disease from the other dogs.
Buck is the largest dog on the team.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The primordial beast is the ancient, wild side of Buck's nature, growing stronger under trail life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Primordial means belonging to the earliest, most ancient stage. The phrase names Buck's reawakening wild instincts.

questions.text: How does Buck finally beat Spitz in their fight to the death?

answers.text: The other dogs help him.
François pulls Spitz away.
He fights by instinct and by head, breaking Spitz's front legs with a trick.
Spitz gives up and runs.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck pretends to try the shoulder trick, then sweeps low and breaks Spitz's legs. He uses imagination, not just instinct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the line "He fought by instinct, but he could fight by head as well." Buck wins with a trick.

questions.text: Which line from Chapter 3 is an example of a SIMILE?

answers.text: "The beast in him roared."
"a wind that cut like a white-hot knife"
"the dominant primordial beast"
"Mercy was a thing reserved for gentler climes."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The word "like" compares the wind to a white-hot knife. That is a simile.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A simile uses "like" or "as" to compare two things. Find the line with one of those words.

questions.text: When London writes that "the cry of Life" plunged "in the grip of Death," he is using:

answers.text: a simile
a fragment
personification
a run-on

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Life and Death are ideas, but London gives them human action and power. That is personification.
questions.feedback_incorrect: London makes ideas like Life and Death act like living things. Giving non-human things human qualities is personification.

questions.text: Which group of words is a complete COMPLEX sentence?

answers.text: Because the beast in him roared.
When Buck finished his ration and returned, he found his nest occupied.
The two dogs snarling in the moonlight.
Buck won the fight the team grew calm.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It joins a dependent clause (When Buck finished his ration and returned) with an independent clause, correctly punctuated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence has one dependent clause and one independent clause. Find the complete one.

questions.text: Which sentence is a RUN-ON that needs to be fixed?

answers.text: Spitz was beaten. Buck became the leader.
After Spitz was beaten, Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten Buck became the leader.
Spitz was beaten, and Buck became the leader.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete thoughts are jammed together with nothing between them. That is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on crowds two complete thoughts together with no period, semicolon, or comma plus conjunction. Find that one.

questions.text: In an argument, after you state a claim and give a quote, what is the job of your EXPLANATION?

answers.text: To add a second quote.
To explain why the quote proves your claim and answer "so what?"
To summarize the whole chapter.
To state your opinion with no evidence.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The explanation connects the quote back to your claim and shows the reader why it matters.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The explanation is where you tie the quote to your claim and answer "so what?" It is what makes the evidence count.

questions.text: Which mark correctly fills the blank? "The dogs were tired ___ the drivers were grumbling."

answers.text: a colon, because a list follows
a semicolon, because a complete sentence follows
a comma, because the two parts are short
no mark is needed

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "The drivers were grumbling" is a complete sentence, so a semicolon joins the two closely related sentences.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at what comes after the blank. It is a complete sentence, so the join is a semicolon.

questions.text: A colon is used correctly when:

answers.text: it joins two complete sentences of equal weight
it separates items inside a list
a complete sentence comes before it and a list or explanation follows
it replaces every comma in a long sentence

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A colon follows a complete sentence and points ahead to a list or an explanation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it and points ahead to a list or explanation.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?

answers.text: "Five dogs remained: Joe, Pike, Sol-leks, Teek, and Buck."
"The dogs that remained were: Joe, Pike, and Buck."
"Five dogs: remained Joe, Pike, and Buck."
"Five dogs remained Joe, Pike: and Buck."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Five dogs remained" is a complete sentence, so the colon can point ahead to the list.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the words before the colon. They must form a complete sentence, like "Five dogs remained."

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?

answers.text: "Because the trail was long; the dogs grew tired."
"The sled was overloaded; the dogs could not move it."
"The owners packed: a tent, dishes, and canned goods."
"Hal whipped the dogs; and Mercedes wept."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A complete sentence sits on each side, so the semicolon joins them correctly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, with no joining word like "and" after it.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a conjunctive adverb?

answers.text: "The trail was long, however the dogs kept moving."
"The sled was overloaded; however, the dogs still tried to pull it."
"The sled was overloaded; however the dogs still tried to pull it."
"However the sled was overloaded, the dogs kept pulling."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A semicolon comes before the conjunctive adverb, and a comma comes right after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the punctuation around "however." It needs a semicolon before it and a comma right after it.

questions.text: Correlative conjunctions are conjunctions that:

answers.text: always end in -ly
come in pairs, with both parts working together
can only join two nouns
replace a subject pronoun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Correlative conjunctions come in pairs, like either...or and not only...but also.
questions.feedback_incorrect: They work in pairs. Think of either...or or both...and.

questions.text: Which word completes the correlative pair? "Neither the dogs ___ the people noticed the spring."

answers.text: or
but
nor
and

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Neither" always pairs with "nor."
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Neither" has one fixed partner. It is "nor."

questions.text: Which sentence uses a correlative conjunction pair correctly?

answers.text: "Both Charles or Hal believed he worked hardest."
"The team would neither pull and stop."
"Not only did they fail to work the dogs, but they failed to work themselves."
"Either the ice was rotten nor the trail was safe."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Not only...but" is a correct correlative pair joining two ideas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Match the partners: both...and, either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also.

questions.text: Which correlative pair best completes this sentence? "Buck would ___ take the lead ___ accept any lesser place."

answers.text: both...and
either...or
neither...but
not only...nor

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Either...or" presents two choices, which fits Buck taking the lead or refusing every other spot.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The sentence offers two choices. The pair that presents a choice is either...or.

questions.text: In Chapter 4, how does Buck finally get the lead position on the team?

answers.text: François rewards him for good behavior.
He refuses every other place until the men give in and let him lead.
Sol-leks gives up the spot willingly from the start.
Perrault trades him for two new dogs.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck will not take any place but the front, circling the camp for nearly an hour until the men let him lead.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the morning after the Spitz fight. Buck demands the lead and refuses every lesser place.

questions.text: After he takes the lead, how does Buck prove he has earned it?

answers.text: He stops working and rests by the fire.
He runs away from the team.
He makes the loafers pull, disciplines the team, and breaks in new dogs fast.
He lets the other dogs do whatever they want.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck makes Pike pull, punishes Joe, and breaks in Teek and Koona so fast it takes the driver's breath away.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at what Buck does on the trail once he leads. He whips the team into shape and proves his mastery.

questions.text: Why does the sick dog Dave fight to stay in the harness even though it is killing him?

answers.text: He is afraid of the other dogs.
He wants to escape the trail.
He does not understand he is hurt.
The pride of trace and trail is his, and he cannot bear another dog doing his work.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London says "the pride of trace and trail was his." The work is who Dave is.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the part where Dave bites through Sol-leks's traces. His pride in the work is the reason.

questions.text: What is the main difference between the skilled drivers and the new owners, Hal, Charles, and Mercedes?

answers.text: The skilled drivers had more money.
The skilled drivers knew the trail and cared for the dogs; the new owners did not know how to work dogs or themselves.
The new owners had better dogs.
The skilled drivers traveled in summer only.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The skilled drivers fed the dogs first and never overloaded the sled. The new owners were ignorant and careless.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Compare how each group treated the dogs and the trail. The difference is knowledge and judgment.

questions.text: Which detail best shows the toil and cruelty of the trail in Chapter 5?

answers.text: The dogs are well fed and rested.
The drivers ride in a heated sled.
The dogs become "perambulating skeletons," so worn that the bite of the whip feels dull and distant.
The team makes a cheerful, easy journey.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. London describes the dogs as walking skeletons, too exhausted to feel the lash. That is the toil of the trail.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the description of how worn down the starving dogs become. The toil is in those harsh details.

questions.text: At the end of Chapter 5, why does John Thornton cut Buck loose from the team?

answers.text: Hal asks him to buy Buck.
Buck has won a fight.
Buck refuses to rise from the rotten ice, and Hal beats him, so Thornton stops Hal to save Buck.
The team needs one fewer dog.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck's instinct keeps him from the rotten ice, and Thornton steps in and cuts him loose, saving his life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the moment Buck will not get up and Thornton stops the beating. Buck's instinct senses the danger.

questions.text: In a strong argument, a counterclaim is best described as:

answers.text: a repeat of your own claim
the strongest fair point against your claim, which you then answer
a list of all your evidence
the very first sentence of the essay

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A counterclaim names the strongest fair opposing point, and then you answer it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A counterclaim states the OTHER side fairly, then you answer it. It is not a repeat of your own claim.

questions.text: Which sentence uses its punctuation correctly?

answers.text: "Five dogs remained; Joe, Pike, Sol-leks, Teek, and Buck."
"Not only did they fail to work the dogs, and they failed to work themselves."
"The sled was overloaded: the dogs could not move it."
"Five dogs remained: Joe, Pike, Sol-leks, Teek, and Buck."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A complete sentence comes before the colon, and a list follows, so the colon is correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it and points ahead to a list. Check which option does that.

questions.text:
Sometimes a noun stands in front of another noun and describes it. Which word is the noun doing an adjective's job in this phrase?

"a river bank"

answers.text: bank
river
a

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. River tells what kind of bank, so the noun river is doing an adjective's job.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what kind of bank?" The word that answers is the noun doing the adjective's job.

questions.text: In "love names," which word is being described (the main noun)?

answers.text: names
love

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Names is the main noun. Love is the noun in front of it, telling what kind.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The main noun is the real thing being talked about. Love is only describing it.

questions.text: A noun is doing an adjective's job when it answers which questions about the noun beside it?

answers.text: How? When? Where?
To what extent?
What kind? Which one?

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Like any adjective, it answers "what kind" or "which one" about a noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "How, when, where" belong to adverbs. A noun doing an adjective's job answers "what kind" or "which one."

questions.text:
Which mark joins two complete sentences that are closely related, without a conjunction?

"Buck loved Thornton fiercely ___ he still heard the wild call."

answers.text: a comma
a semicolon
a colon
a question mark

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both sides are complete sentences, so a semicolon joins them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each side can stand alone as a sentence. The mark that joins two complete sentences is the semicolon.

questions.text:
Which mark says "here it comes" and introduces a list after a complete sentence?

"Three dogs loafed by the river ___ Buck, Skeet, and Nig."

answers.text: a colon
a semicolon
a comma

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A colon introduces the list that follows the complete sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The blank comes right before a list. The mark that introduces a list is the colon.

questions.text: Which sentence uses commas correctly to separate items in a list?

answers.text: Skeet Nig and Buck romped together.
Skeet, Nig, and Buck romped together.
Skeet; Nig; and Buck romped together.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Commas separate the items in a list.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Items in a simple list are separated by commas, not semicolons or nothing at all.

questions.text:
Thornton shouts an urgent command above the rapids. Which end mark best fits?

"Go, Buck ___"

answers.text: a period
a comma
an exclamation point

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A shouted, urgent command takes an exclamation point: "Go, Buck!"
questions.feedback_incorrect: He is shouting an urgent command. The end mark for a strong cry is the exclamation point.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: This man had saved his life, he was the ideal master.
This man had saved his life; he was the ideal master.
This man had saved his life: he was, the ideal master.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete sentences joined without a conjunction need a semicolon, not a comma.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma is a run-on. Use a semicolon between them.

questions.text: Who is John Thornton, and why does he matter to Buck in Chapter 6?

answers.text: A cruel driver who beats Buck.
The man who saves Buck's life and whom Buck loves for the first time.
Another sled dog on the team.
The judge who first owned Buck in California.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Thornton rescues Buck and becomes the first person Buck ever truly loves.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening of Chapter 6. Thornton is the man who nursed Buck back to health and won his love.

questions.text: London writes that the call lured Buck into the forest, but "the love for John Thornton drew him back to the fire again." What does this show?

answers.text: Buck no longer feels the call of the wild at all.
Two forces are pulling on Buck at the same time, and the love pulls him back.
Buck has fully become a wild wolf.
Thornton wants Buck to leave.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The wild pulls Buck toward the forest, and his love for Thornton pulls him back. He is caught between the two.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Notice that both forces act on Buck. The call pulls one way; the love pulls the other.

questions.text: Which detail shows that Buck is still wild even while he loves Thornton?

answers.text: Buck lies at Thornton's feet for hours.
Buck lets Skeet clean his wounds.
Buck shows no mercy to strange dogs and still hears the wild call.
Buck follows Thornton out of the tent.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Buck fights other dogs without mercy and still feels the call, proof the wild is alive in him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the moment that shows the primitive, not the tame. The love details show the opposite.

questions.text: Why does Buck attack "Black" Burton in the saloon?

answers.text: Burton steals Buck's food.
Burton strikes John Thornton.
Burton is another sled driver.
Buck wants to leave the camp.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The moment Burton hits Thornton, Buck springs at his throat. His love drives him to protect his master.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the saloon scene. Buck moves the instant someone hurts Thornton.

questions.text: This week's poem tells a grim story but feels lively and even funny. Which part of the poem's FORM creates that feeling?

answers.text: Its long, plain sentences with no pattern.
Its swinging beat and chiming rhymes.
Its lack of any characters.
Its missing ending.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The bouncy beat and the rhymes give a dark story a wild, almost cheerful energy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what made the poem fun to say aloud. The beat and the rhyme shape the tone.

questions.text: What is the job of a repeated line (a refrain) in a story-poem?

answers.text: It hides the poem's meaning.
It works like a chorus and drives home the main feeling each time it returns.
It ends the poem early.
It tells the reader to stop.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Like a song's chorus, the repeated line returns and presses the main feeling on the reader.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think of a song. The line that comes back, the chorus, is what sticks and carries the feeling.

questions.text: In the phrase "river bank," which word is a noun doing an adjective's job?

answers.text: bank
river
the

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. River tells what kind of bank, so the noun river is doing an adjective's job.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what kind of bank?" The word that answers is the noun acting like an adjective.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: This man had saved his life, he was the ideal master.
This man had saved his life he was the ideal master.
This man had saved his life; he was the ideal master.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two complete sentences joined without a conjunction need a semicolon between them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Joining two complete sentences with only a comma, or with nothing, is an error. Use a semicolon.

quizzes.title: Module 2 Outro — Looking Back
quizzes.description: You have finished the reading and the project work for Module 2. Take a few minutes to look back. Answer honestly. This is how your teacher learns what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. Look back at how you answered this in the Module Intro: **What transforms Buck from a pampered house dog into a creature of the wild, and what does his change reveal about instinct, survival, and the pull between civilization and the wild?

Answer it again now, in three or four sentences, using something specific from Buck's story (for example, the law of club and fang, his fight with Spitz, his love for John Thornton, or the ending). How has your answer changed since the start?

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)
Confidence rating. How confident do you feel that you can make an argument about Buck's transformation and back it up with details from the book, including a thesis, evidence, and a counterclaim?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about The Call of the Wild, the theme of civilization versus the wild, or the argument-writing skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. This module is about survival, hardship, and transformation. Pick the ONE virtue Buck most needed to survive and grow, and that this module asked of you:

answers.text: Perseverance (pushing on through brutal toil and not giving up)
Courage (facing danger, the club, the fight with Spitz, the wild)
Self-government (learning the new rules and mastering his own instincts)
Another of the seven virtues

questions.text: Explain your choice above in two or three sentences.

quizzes.title: Module 3 Intro — Before We Begin
quizzes.description: Welcome to Module 3. You will read A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens, a short novella about a bitter, cold-hearted miser named Ebenezer Scrooge who is visited by three spirits on Christmas Eve. By morning, something has changed in him. Before you begin, answer a few quick questions. There are no wrong answers here. Your first thoughts give your teacher a starting point.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **What changes Scrooge: fear, memory, or love, and can a person truly change?

In two or three sentences, give your first answer. You have not read the novella yet, so just say what you think right now: what do you believe actually changes a person, and is that change ever permanent? You will come back to this question again at the end.

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. By the end of this module you will be able to:

- [ ] Read and follow the events of A Christmas Carol across all five staves, from Marley's ghost to Scrooge's transformation. - [ ] Explain how Dickens uses the three spirits to show different forces that can change a person: memory, fear of consequences, and generosity. - [ ] Notice and name craft moves such as figurative language, symbol, and tone, and find them in the text. - [ ] Build one Reading Journal all module long and use it to develop your thinking about the central theme. - [ ] Design a book cover that captures the novella's theme and write a reflection explaining your choices with evidence from the text.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
One thing you are curious about. Name one thing about Scrooge, about ghosts and memory, or about this story that you are curious to find out. One sentence is fine.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal.)
Which sentence is a comma splice?

answers.text: Scrooge worked late into the evening, and he sent Bob home with a reluctant nod.
Marley was dead Scrooge had never changed the sign on the door.
Scrooge paid Bob very little, but Bob was grateful for the work.
Scrooge worked late into the evening, Bob sat shivering at his tiny candle.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone: that is a comma splice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma and no conjunction. Find the option where the comma has nothing after it to join the two clauses.

questions.text: Which sentence is a run-on sentence?

answers.text: Scrooge dismissed the charity collectors; he wanted nothing to do with their request.
The Ghost arrived at midnight Scrooge could not look away from the glowing figure.
Marley had been dead for seven years, yet Scrooge still kept his partner's name above the door.
Although Scrooge was wealthy, he lived as though he had nothing.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two independent clauses with nothing between them at all: that is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on has no punctuation between two independent clauses. Look for the option where two complete thoughts crash into each other with no separator.

questions.text: What is the difference between a comma splice and a run-on sentence?

answers.text: A comma splice has too many commas; a run-on has no verbs.
A comma splice is always longer than a run-on.
A comma splice joins two independent clauses with a comma only; a run-on joins them with no punctuation at all.
A run-on uses a semicolon incorrectly; a comma splice uses a period incorrectly.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. That is the key distinction. Both are errors involving independent clauses; they differ in what (if anything) is between them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what is placed between the two independent clauses in each error type. One uses a comma alone; the other uses nothing.

questions.text:
Which option correctly fixes this comma splice?

"Marley's ghost appeared at midnight, Scrooge trembled in his bed."

answers.text: Marley's ghost appeared at midnight; Scrooge trembled in his bed.
Marley's ghost appeared at midnight, but, Scrooge trembled in his bed.
Marley's ghost appeared at midnight Scrooge trembled in his bed.
Marley's ghost appeared at midnight. but Scrooge trembled in his bed.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A semicolon correctly separates two independent clauses. No additional conjunction is needed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To fix a comma splice, you can use a period, a semicolon, or add a coordinating conjunction after the comma. Which option does one of those things correctly?

questions.text:
Which option correctly fixes this run-on sentence?

"The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school Scrooge recognized the empty classroom."

answers.text: The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school, Scrooge recognized the empty classroom.
The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school. Scrooge recognized the empty classroom.
The Spirit showed Scrooge, his old school Scrooge recognized the empty classroom.
The Spirit showed Scrooge his old school and, Scrooge recognized the empty classroom.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A period ends the first independent clause cleanly and starts the second as its own sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: To fix a run-on, add proper punctuation between the two independent clauses. A period, a semicolon, or a comma plus conjunction all work. Find the option that does this correctly.

questions.text: Which sentence from the choices below is correctly written (no comma splice, no run-on)?

answers.text: Belle released Scrooge from their engagement he watched her go without a word.
Scrooge watched the Fezziwig party, he wished he could speak to his own clerk.
The counting-house was cold, for Scrooge kept the coal box locked and Bob had only a candle.
The Spirit pointed Scrooge followed it out the window into the night air.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The coordinating conjunction "for" after the comma correctly joins the two independent clauses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A correct sentence either has just one independent clause, or it joins two independent clauses with proper punctuation and/or a conjunction. Find the option that does this correctly.

questions.text:
In this sentence, what part of speech is the subject noun of the first independent clause?

"Scrooge kept the coal box locked; Bob shivered at his single candle."

answers.text: verb
adjective
subject noun
preposition

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Scrooge is a proper noun serving as the subject noun of the first independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "Who or what kept the coal box locked?" The answer names a person. What part of speech names a person?

questions.text:
Which word in the sentence below is a linking verb?

"Scrooge was his sole executor, his sole administrator, his sole residuary legatee, his sole friend, and his sole mourner."

answers.text: sole
mourner
was
his

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Was" links the subject noun Scrooge to the list of nouns that describe his relationship to Marley. It is a linking verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "What is being said about Scrooge?" The word that connects him to the description is the linking verb.

questions.text: At the opening of Stave 1, Dickens describes Scrooge by saying "The cold within him froze his old features." What does this description show about Scrooge?

answers.text: He is physically ill.
He is afraid of the winter weather.
His greed and coldness of character show on his body and affect everyone around him.
He lives in a poorly heated house.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The cold comes from inside Scrooge. It is his character, not the weather.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Dickens says the cold is "within him." What does that tell you about where Scrooge's coldness comes from?

questions.text: In Stave 1, Marley's ghost says: "I wear the chain I forged in life. I made it link by link, and yard by yard." What does the chain represent?

answers.text: The literal chains Marley was buried in.
The consequences of the selfish choices Marley made during his lifetime.
The money Marley owed to Scrooge.
The punishment Marley received from a judge.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The chain is a metaphor for a life spent in greed and selfishness. Each link is a bad choice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Marley says he "forged" it himself. What kind of choices build a chain like that?

questions.text: In Stave 2, the Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge three memories. Which of these is one of them?

answers.text: The death of Scrooge's mother when he was a baby.
Scrooge working late on Christmas Eve while Bob Cratchit went home.
Old Fezziwig's Christmas party, where Scrooge was a young apprentice.
Scrooge and Marley founding their business together.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Fezziwig party is one of the three key memories in Stave 2. Scrooge worked there as a young man.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the three memories the Spirit shows Scrooge in Stave 2. Which of these actually appears?

questions.text: After seeing the Fezziwig party in Stave 2, Scrooge says he wishes he could "say a word or two" to his clerk. What does this moment show?

answers.text: Scrooge wants to fire Bob Cratchit.
Scrooge is starting to feel regret about how he treats Bob, comparing himself to Fezziwig.
Scrooge wants to invite Bob to a party.
Scrooge is proud of his own business and wants to boast about it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Scrooge sees himself in Fezziwig's role as an employer and realizes how far he falls short.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what Fezziwig represented to his workers. Scrooge is comparing himself to that. What does the comparison reveal?

questions.text: Which sentence is a comma splice?

answers.text: Scrooge refused the donation; the collectors left without a coin.
Although Marley was dead, his name remained on the door.
The Spirit arrived, Scrooge trembled and could not look away.
Scrooge worked on Christmas Eve and dismissed his nephew with a word.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone: "The Spirit arrived" and "Scrooge trembled and could not look away."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. Find the option where both sides could stand alone as full sentences.

questions.text: Which sentence is a run-on sentence?

answers.text: Scrooge was his own sole mourner, yet he never gave it a second thought.
Belle released Scrooge from their engagement he watched her go in silence.
The counting-house was cold; Scrooge kept the coal box locked.
When the bell struck one, Scrooge waited for the Spirit to appear.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two independent clauses with nothing between them: that is a run-on.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on has no punctuation at all between two independent clauses. Which option has two complete thoughts crashing together with nothing to separate them?

questions.text: Belle says Scrooge has let "another idol" take her place. What type of figurative language is this?

answers.text: Simile
Personification
Alliteration
Metaphor

questions.feedback_correct: Right. She calls money an "idol" directly, without using "like" or "as." That is a metaphor.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A metaphor is a direct comparison without "like" or "as." Is Belle comparing money to an idol using "like," or is she calling it an idol outright?

questions.text: Which of the following is a theme statement (not just a topic) for Staves 1-2?

answers.text: Greed.
Memory is an important part of life.
A Christmas Carol is about ghosts and the past.
Greed destroys human connection, and only honest memory can begin to undo that damage.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A theme statement makes a complete claim about what the text argues, not just a label for what it is about.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A topic is a label (like "greed"). A theme statement is a complete sentence that says something specific about the topic. Which option does that?

questions.text: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?

answers.text: The Ghost's robe was green and free.
The Ghosts robe was green and free.
The Ghost'es robe was green and free.
The Ghosts' robe was green and free.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ghost's uses an apostrophe + s to show that the robe belongs to the Ghost.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A singular possessive noun adds apostrophe + s. The robe belongs to one Ghost: Ghost's.

questions.text: "The Spirits torch lit the room." What is the error?

answers.text: The word lit should be lighted.
The word Spirits needs an apostrophe to show the torch belongs to the Spirit.
The word room needs a capital letter.
There is no error in this sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Spirit's torch uses an apostrophe + s to show ownership.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask: does a noun in this sentence show ownership? That noun needs apostrophe + s.

questions.text: Which sentence uses its and it's correctly?

answers.text: Its a cold Christmas morning in the city.
The Spirit closed it's robe around the children.
The Spirit opened its robe; it's cold outside.
The city its quiet on Christmas morning.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Its (possessive pronoun, no apostrophe) and it's (it is, has apostrophe) are both correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Its shows ownership by a pronoun and has no apostrophe. It's is a contraction for it is and has an apostrophe.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a contraction?

answers.text: Scrooge hadn't felt this way in many years.
Scrooge hadnt felt this way in many years.
Scrooge had'nt felt this way in many years.
Scrooge hadn't' felt this way in many years.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Hadn't correctly places the apostrophe where the letter o is left out (had not).
questions.feedback_incorrect: A contraction places the apostrophe exactly where letters were removed. Had + not = hadn't.

questions.text: Parallel structure means the items in a list or series all use the same grammatical form. Which sentence has a parallel structure error?

answers.text: Scrooge laughed, cried, and danced in the street.
He sent a turkey, raised Bob's salary, and promised to help the family.
Scrooge became a good friend, a good master, and good.
The Spirit pointed, waited, and vanished.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The series breaks at the end: a good friend, a good master, and good. It should be a good man to match the pattern.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the form of each item in the list. Does each one follow the same pattern? Look for the one that breaks the pattern.

questions.text:
Which sentence corrects the parallel structure error?

"Scrooge became generous, kind, and a joyful man."

answers.text: Scrooge became generous, kind, and joy.
Scrooge became generous, kind, and joyful.
Scrooge became a generous man, kind, and joyful.
Scrooge became generously, kindly, and joyful.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Generous, kind, and joyful are all adjectives -- the list is now parallel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each item in the list needs to be the same part of speech. Generous and kind are adjectives, so the third item should be an adjective too.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?

answers.text: The Spirit showed Scrooge joy, sorrow, and being afraid.
The Spirit showed Scrooge joy, sorrow, and to fear.
The Spirit showed Scrooge joy, sorrow, and fear.
The Spirit showed Scrooge joyful, sorrow, and fear.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Joy, sorrow, and fear are all nouns -- the list is parallel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Match the form of each item. If the first two are nouns (joy, sorrow), the third should also be a noun.

questions.text: Which sentence from Stave 5 has correct parallel structure AND correct apostrophe use?

answers.text: Scrooge became Bob's friend, his employer, and good to him.
Scrooge became Bob's friend, Bob's employer, and Bob's second father.
Scrooge became Bobs friend, his employer, and a father figure.
Scrooge became a friend to Bob, employer, and was a father.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The list is parallel (three noun phrases with the same structure) and Bob's has the apostrophe in the right place.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check both: does each list item follow the same form? Does the possessive noun have its apostrophe?

questions.text: In Stave 3, the Ghost of Christmas Present shows Scrooge two ragged children hidden in its robe. What are their names?

answers.text: Greed and Pride
Past and Future
Ignorance and Want
Shadow and Doom

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Spirit names them: "This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want."
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Spirit names the children directly before it vanishes. Look for the two words it uses.

questions.text: At the Cratchit Christmas table, Bob proposes a toast to Scrooge as "Founder of the Feast." How does Mrs. Cratchit respond?

answers.text: She drinks the toast gladly to honor her husband's employer.
She refuses to drink at all and leaves the table.
She drinks it reluctantly, for Bob's sake and for the day, calling Scrooge "odious" and "stingy."
She laughs and agrees that Scrooge deserves to be honored.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. She says she will drink "for your sake and the Day's, not for his," and calls him "an odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling man."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Mrs. Cratchit does drink the toast, but not willingly. What does she call Scrooge while doing it?

questions.text: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come is different from the other two spirits in a key way. What is it?

answers.text: It shows Scrooge scenes from his childhood.
It is cheerful and speaks freely to Scrooge.
It is silent and communicates only by pointing.
It shows Scrooge scenes from other people's lives only, never his own.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Spirit never speaks. Its only gesture is a pointing hand.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how this Spirit communicates compared to the other two. Does it speak?

questions.text: At the end of Stave 4, Scrooge kneels at a neglected grave. What does he read on the headstone?

answers.text: Jacob Marley
Ebenezer Scrooge
Tiny Tim Cratchit
Bob Cratchit

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Ghost points to the stone and Scrooge reads his own name: EBENEZER SCROOGE.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Spirit has been pointing to this grave for much of Stave 4. Whose name does Scrooge finally read?

questions.text: In Stave 5, what is the first generous act Scrooge performs on Christmas morning?

answers.text: He visits Bob Cratchit's family and gives them money.
He goes to his nephew Fred's house for Christmas dinner.
He donates to the charity collectors he turned away the day before.
He sends the prize turkey anonymously to the Cratchit family.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. He buys the prize turkey -- "twice the size of Tiny Tim" -- and sends it to Bob's anonymously.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Scrooge's very first act of generosity happens before he even leaves his house. What does he do with the turkey?

questions.text: Which sentence uses apostrophes correctly?

answers.text: Scrooges heart was changed by the Spirits lessons.
Scrooge's heart was changed by the Spirits' lessons.
Scrooge's heart was changed by the Spirit's lessons.
Scrooges heart was changed by the Spirit's lessons.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Scrooge's (one Scrooge owns the heart) and Spirit's (one Spirit gives the lesson) are both correctly punctuated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each possessive noun: does it have an apostrophe + s? Which option gets both right?

questions.text: Which sentence has correct parallel structure?

answers.text: Scrooge became kind, generous, and he had warmth.
Scrooge became kind, generous, and warmed by life.
Scrooge became kind, generous, and warm.
Scrooge became kindly, generous, and warm.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Kind, generous, and warm are all adjectives -- the list is parallel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each item in the list needs the same form. Which option keeps all three items as simple adjectives?

questions.text: Dickens ends A Christmas Carol with Tiny Tim's words: "God bless Us, Every One!" Why does this line work as a closing for the story?

answers.text: It shows that Tiny Tim has forgotten everything Scrooge did to the family.
It reminds the reader that Tiny Tim is the real hero of the story, not Scrooge.
It suggests that Scrooge's change matters beyond himself: the most vulnerable character survives and offers a blessing to everyone.
It is simply a traditional Victorian way to end a Christmas story.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Tiny Tim was the child whose death Scrooge's change prevents. His survival and his blessing show that transformation has consequences beyond the person who changes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what Tiny Tim represents in the story and how his final words connect to the theme of generosity and what Scrooge's change makes possible.

quizzes.title: Module 3 Outro — Looking Back
quizzes.description: You have finished the reading and the project work for Module 3. Take a few minutes to look back at Scrooge and at your own work. Answer honestly. This is how your teacher learns what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. Look back at how you answered this in the Module Intro: **What changes Scrooge: fear, memory, or love, and can a person truly change?

Answer it again now, in three or four sentences, using something specific from the novella. You might point to a moment with the Ghost of Christmas Past, a scene with Tiny Tim and the Cratchits, or the vision of Scrooge's own neglected grave. How has your answer changed since the start?

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)
Confidence rating. How confident do you feel that you can explain the central theme of A Christmas Carol and support your reading with specific details from the text?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about A Christmas Carol, the theme of generosity and change, or the project skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. This module is about a person who changes from selfish isolation to generosity toward others. Pick the ONE virtue Scrooge most needed to change, and that this module asked of you:

answers.text: Service (choosing to give your time and resources to others, the way Scrooge does at the end)
Responsibility (owning the harm your choices have caused and correcting course)
Honesty (facing the truth about yourself, even when it is painful)
Another of the seven virtues

questions.text: Explain your choice above in two or three sentences.

discussions.title: Module 1 - Gulliver's Travels - All-Class Forum 1: A Merciful Sentence
discussions.html:
All-Class Forum 1 · A Merciful Sentence
MODULE 1 · GULLIVER'S TRAVELS · PART I, CH. 7
25 pointsPost + 2 repliesReplies stay hidden until you postCloses end of Week 3
The scene
 
›Articles of impeachment are drawn up against Gulliver at the Lilliputian court.
›Some of the council want him put to death.
›Reldresal, who is called Gulliver's friend, speaks in his favour.
›What Reldresal proposes instead of death is that Gulliver's eyes be put out.
›The court receives this as the merciful option, and adds that he should then be starved by degrees.
The question
 
Reldresal argues for blinding Gulliver and calls it mercy. Is he acting as Gulliver's friend?
Both answers can be argued from Chapter 7. Take the one you can support.
Your first post
 
1
Take a side in the first sentence.
Friend, or not. No build-up.
2
Quote what Reldresal actually says.
The speech is in Chapter 7. Cite it as (Swift, Part I, Ch. 7).
3
State what his proposal would cost Gulliver.
Be specific. Blindness is not the whole of it.
4
Answer the strongest objection to your own side.
Friend: he is the only person in the room arguing for Gulliver to live. Not a friend: he opens by agreeing that Gulliver is guilty.
Reldresal presents the council with two outcomes, death or blinding, as though those were the only two available. Add one sentence: what is wrong with reasoning that way, and what third option was open to him?

discussions.html:
All-Class Forum 2 · One Witness
MODULE 1 · GULLIVER'S TRAVELS · PART II, CH. 6
25 pointsPost + 2 repliesReplies stay hidden until you postCloses end of Week 5
The scene
 
›Over several audiences, Gulliver describes England to the king of Brobdingnag.
›He is trying to impress him, and he chooses what to include.
›The king asks questions and keeps asking.
›At the end of it the king delivers a verdict on the whole of Gulliver's countrymen, and it is a crushing one.
The question
 
The king reaches a conclusion about a whole nation from one man's account. Was that conclusion earned?
This is not about whether the king is right about people. It is about whether his evidence could support the conclusion he drew.
Your first post
 
1
Take a side in the first sentence.
Earned, or not earned. No build-up.
2
Name what the king actually had to work with.
One witness, and a proud one. Cite the chapter as (Swift, Part II, Ch. 6).
3
Name one thing Gulliver left out or dressed up.
From the text of his account, not from your own knowledge of England.
4
Answer the strongest objection to your own side.
Earned: Gulliver volunteered the worst of it himself, under questioning. Not earned: the king never heard from anybody else.
The king draws a conclusion about millions of people from a single boastful witness. Add one sentence: what is wrong with reasoning that way, and what would have had to be true for the conclusion to hold?

discussions.title: Module Discussion: Gulliver's Travels
discussions.html:
Pride and human nature in Gulliver's Travels.

By now Gulliver has been a giant among tiny people and a tiny person among giants, and he has heard the king of Brobdingnag judge humankind harshly. Across these voyages, Swift keeps holding up a mirror to human pride.

Your post (one short paragraph): State one claim about what Swift is saying about human pride or human nature. Then explain why you believe it, using one specific detail or moment from the reading so far. For example, you might claim that Swift thinks people look foolish when they take themselves too seriously, and then point to the way the tiny Lilliputians act about their grand titles.

Your reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add a second piece of evidence that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, using the text.

Keep your post to about five to seven sentences. Keep your reply to two or three.

Posting rules

  • Post your own claim first, before you can see classmates' posts (set the Canvas option to require an initial post).
  • Use at least one specific detail from the reading. A claim with no evidence is not finished.
  • Be respectful in disagreement. Argue with the idea, not the person.

All-Class Forum 1 · The Circle Closes
MODULE 2 · THE CALL OF THE WILD · CH. 3
25 pointsPost + 2 repliesReplies stay hidden until you postCloses end of Week 3
The scene
 
›Buck and Spitz fight for the last time.
›Spitz slips, and Buck breaks through his defence.
›The watching huskies close into a circle around Spitz.
›Buck stands back and does not finish it himself.
›London calls Buck the successful champion, and says he found it good.
The question
 
Buck steps back and lets the circle finish Spitz. Does that make the kill his?
Both readings are defensible from Chapter 3. Take the one you can support from the words.
Your first post
 
1
Take a side in the first sentence.
His, or not his. No build-up.
2
Say exactly what Buck does and does not do.
The text is precise about this. Cite it as (London, Ch. 3).
3
Say what London's own wording commits him to.
He calls Buck the champion and says he found it good. Take that seriously as evidence.
4
Answer the strongest objection to your own side.
His: he started it, he chose the moment, and he wanted the outcome. Not his: he never delivered the blow, and the pack had its own reasons.
A reader can defend Buck by saying this is simply the law of that world. Add one sentence: does calling something the law settle whether it was right, and why or why not?

All-Class Forum 2 · Dave in the Traces
MODULE 2 · THE CALL OF THE WILD · CH. 5
25 pointsPost + 2 repliesReplies stay hidden until you postCloses end of Week 4
The scene
 
›Dave is sick, and it is plain to everyone that the work is killing him.
›The drivers cut him out of the traces so he can run free behind the sled.
›Dave will not have it. He struggles, and he bites through another dog's traces to get back to his place.
›They put him back in the harness.
›He pulls until he cannot, and later a shot is heard behind the column.
The question
 
Dave asks to keep working, and the work kills him. Were the drivers right to put him back in the harness?
The text gives real reasons on both sides. Take the one you can support.
Your first post
 
1
Take a side in the first sentence.
Right, or not right. No build-up.
2
Say what Dave does when he is cut loose.
The detail matters. Cite it as (London, Ch. 5).
3
Say what the drivers understood at the time.
Not what a reader knows at the end of the chapter.
4
Answer the strongest objection to your own side.
Right: it was the only thing he still wanted, and they gave it to him. Not right: they were the ones who knew what it would cost, and he was not.
The drivers act as though there were only two possibilities, harness or discard. Add one sentence: what is wrong with reasoning that way, and what third possibility was open?

discussions.title: Module Discussion: The Call of the Wild
discussions.html:
Transformation and the call of the wild in The Call of the Wild.

By now Buck has gone from a pampered house dog at Judge Miller's place to a sled dog who has learned the law of club and fang, beaten Spitz for the lead, and survived a cruel trail. He has also found something he never had before: love for a man, John Thornton. Across the book, Buck is pulled in two directions, toward people and toward the wild.

Your post (one short paragraph): State one claim about Buck's transformation. For example, you might claim that the wild does not destroy Buck but reveals what he always was, or you might claim that the cruelty of the Northland is what truly changes him. Then explain why you believe it, using one specific detail or moment from the reading so far (for example, the club scene, the fight with Spitz, the death of an exhausted dog on the trail, or Buck dragging the sled for Thornton).

Your reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add a second piece of evidence that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, using the text.

discussions.title: Module Discussion: A Christmas Carol
discussions.html:
Can a person truly change? What Scrooge's story says.

By now you have met Scrooge at his worst: refusing charity, dismissing his nephew's invitation, letting his clerk shiver in the cold. You have seen Marley's ghost arrive in chains forged from a lifetime of selfishness. And you have watched the Ghost of Christmas Past drag Scrooge back through memories he had buried. Something is shifting in him. But what is doing the work?

Your post (one short paragraph): State one claim about what it takes for a person to truly change. Then explain why you believe it, using one specific moment from A Christmas Carol so far. For example, you might claim that Scrooge begins to change only because he is afraid of what he will become, and point to his reaction when he sees the chained ghost of his old partner. Or you might claim that the key is not fear but memory, and point to the scene where the young Scrooge is shown sitting alone at school while his classmates go home for the holidays.

Your reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add a second piece of evidence that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, using the text.

All-Class Forum 1 · Answer Scrooge
MODULE 3 · A CHRISTMAS CAROL · STAVE 1
25 pointsPost + 2 repliesReplies stay hidden until you postCloses end of Week 1
The scene
 
›Two gentlemen come to Scrooge's counting-house collecting for the poor.
›Scrooge does not simply refuse them. He argues.
›He asks whether there are prisons and workhouses, and says the Poor Law is in full vigour.
›He says he already helps to support those establishments, and that they cost enough.
›Told that many would rather die than go there, he says that if they would rather die, they had better do it.
The question
 
Scrooge gives reasons, not just refusals. Which of his reasons is hardest to answer, and how do you answer it?
Pick one reason. A post that dismisses all of them at once has answered none of them.
Your first post
 
1
Name the reason you are taking on, in the first sentence.
Quote it. Cite it as (Dickens, Stave 1).
2
Say why that one is the hardest.
Harder than the others, not merely the worst. Those are different claims.
3
Answer it.
Not by describing Scrooge. By answering the reason itself.
4
Say what your answer does not settle.
One sentence. An honest limit is worth more than a clean win.
Scrooge's reasons come in an order, and each one leans on the one before it. Add one sentence: which reason is holding the others up, and what happens to the rest if that one fails?
Other posts stay hidden until yours is submitted. That is deliberate.

Add
One more piece of evidence for their claim that they did not use.
Challenge
Name the part of their reasoning you think is wrong, and say why.
Ask
A question their post left open, in a form they could answer.
Look for a post that took a different side, or your side for a different reason.

→Name a moment. Chapter and scene, not “the book shows.”
→“I agree” is not a reply. Add, challenge, or ask.
→Argue the idea, not the person. Changing your mind in public is permitted.
→Do not restate. If someone made your point, take it further or take another side.

☐One reason is named and quoted in the first sentence, with a citation.
☐Why that reason is the hardest is stated, not merely that it is the worst.
☐The reason itself is answered, rather than the man described.
☐One thing the answer does not settle is named.
☐The sentence about which reason holds the others up is included.

discussions.html:
All-Class Forum 2 · His Own Words Back
MODULE 3 · A CHRISTMAS CAROL · STAVES 1 AND 3
25 pointsPost + 2 repliesReplies stay hidden until you postCloses end of Week 2
The scene
 
›In Stave 1 Scrooge asks whether there are no prisons and no workhouses.
›In Stave 3 the Ghost of Christmas Present shows him two starving children.
›When Scrooge asks whether nothing can be done for them, the Ghost answers by giving him his own words back.
›The Ghost does not argue with what Scrooge said. It repeats it.
The question
 
The Ghost answers Scrooge by quoting Scrooge. Does that answer his argument, or only shame the man who made it?
A reply can be devastating and still not be an answer. Decide which this is.
Your first post
 
1
Take a side in the first sentence.
Answers it, or only shames him. No build-up.
2
Put the two moments side by side.
Cite both, as (Dickens, Stave 1) and (Dickens, Stave 3).
3
Say what the Ghost's reply does to Scrooge, and what it leaves standing.
Both halves. One half is half an answer.
4
Answer the strongest objection to your own side.
An answer: hearing his words in front of the children IS the refutation, because it shows what they meant. Only shame: the reply never touches his claim about who should pay.
Turning a person's words back on them can expose a bad argument, and it can also skip past a real one. Add one sentence: what would the Ghost have had to say to answer the argument itself?

Add
One more piece of evidence for their claim that they did not use.
Challenge
Name the part of their reasoning you think is wrong, and say why.
Ask
A question their post left open, in a form they could answer.
Look for a post that took a different side, or your side for a different reason.
How we argue here
 
→Name a moment. Chapter and scene, not “the book shows.”
→“I agree” is not a reply. Add, challenge, or ask.
→Argue the idea, not the person. Changing your mind in public is permitted.

☐The first sentence takes a side.
☐Both moments are cited, one from Stave 1 and one from Stave 3.
☐Both halves are covered: what the reply does, and what it leaves standing.
